risks.rationale: Placing PII with a third-party provider adds another entity that must be trusted to protect it.

risks.description: PII shared through third-party applications is not periodically purged, increasing the chance that stale records remain available longer than necessary.
risks.evidence_quote: 10.6 Is the PII that becomes available through the agency’s use of 3rd party websites and/or applications purged periodically? • No
risks.rationale: Longer persistence of personal data increases exposure over time and makes accidental disclosure more likely.

risks.description: The system retains records for long periods, which can prolong exposure of personal information even after the original business need has ended.
risks.evidence_quote: All information contained will be retained in compliance with NARA Guidelines, which vary from five to ten years according to the NARA General Records Schedules Transmittal 29, issued December 2017.
risks.rationale: Extended retention increases the window during which a record can be accessed, misused, or breached.

risks.description: Users can upload documents and photos and manually store information from public web applications, so there is a risk that more PII than necessary will be collected and retained in file form.
risks.evidence_quote: Users can upload documents and photos to a shared files folder, determine how their content can be shared with other users, and invite others to view and/or edit shared files.
risks.rationale: A flexible file-sharing system can encourage overcollection because it accepts whatever content users choose to upload.

mitigations.description: Continue using encryption in transit and at rest for stored files, and keep strong access controls around sensitive uploads.
mitigations.evidence_quote: FPAC Box compliments secure file transfer, storage and archiving in a FedRAMP certified environment which utilizes encryption in transit and at rest.
mitigations.rationale: Encryption and access controls reduce the likelihood that highly sensitive files can be read if intercepted or improperly accessed.

mitigations.description: Enforce need-to-know access through role-based authorization and audit access to shared files.
mitigations.evidence_quote: FPAC Box will provide the following capabilities: Unlimited Data Storage • Robust access control and audit capabilities
mitigations.rationale: Limiting and reviewing access helps prevent unnecessary disclosure to authorized but uninvolved users.

mitigations.description: Require the vendor to maintain strong contractual and security safeguards for any PII handled through the third-party cloud service.
mitigations.rationale: A third-party host should be bound to clear security obligations because the system relies on the vendor to secure some PII.

mitigations.description: Implement periodic purge or records-review processes for third-party application data so stale PII is removed when no longer needed.
mitigations.rationale: Regular deletion or review reduces the amount of old personal data left exposed in connected applications.

mitigations.description: Apply records schedules and disable accounts promptly when users leave so retained data and access do not persist longer than necessary.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Individuals have control of the shelf life for retention. If the user leaves, their account gets disabled.
mitigations.rationale: Tying retention and access to lifecycle events reduces unnecessary long-term exposure.

mitigations.description: Limit uploads to only the documents needed for the mission and provide user guidance on minimizing PII in shared files.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing uploaded content reduces the amount of personal information the system can expose.

risks.description: Information sent through the system to DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov could be intercepted or exposed in transit, revealing user data involved in H2A applications.
risks.evidence_quote: As a result, information will be sent to (and from) users (farmers and producers) to DOL and USCIS, even though FPAC CASP / H2A does not assess or perform any actions on the data.
risks.rationale: Any system that forwards user information to external agencies creates privacy risk if transmission is not adequately protected.

risks.description: Using a single common entry point concentrates access to multiple federal services, increasing the privacy impact if the entry point is misused or compromised.
risks.evidence_quote: FPAC CASP / H2A is, however, used as a ‘pass through’ system to allow farmers and producers to access DOL and USCIS from a single (common) entry point.
risks.rationale: A single access point can expose more user activity and facilitate broader unauthorized access if compromised.

risks.description: The retained DOL case number could still be linked to a producer’s inquiry and reveal participation in the H2A process if improperly accessed.
risks.evidence_quote: The only user information that is stored on FPAC CASP is a producer’s DOL case number; this information does not identify the specific user or contain any user information. This DOL case number is retained in FAPC CASP for 90 days.
risks.rationale: Even limited retained identifiers can become privacy-relevant when they can be associated with a person’s application activity.

risks.description: The system relies on data collected by external services, so users may not have clear visibility into what information is collected and how it is handled once it leaves FPAC CASP.
risks.evidence_quote: Data is transmitted through FPAC CASP / H2A by users (farmers and producers), US Department of Labor, and United States Citizenship and Immigration Services.
risks.rationale: When data is collected by other agencies through a pass-through system, users may lose direct control and understanding of their information.

mitigations.description: Continue to require HTTPS for communications between FPAC CASP / H2A and the external services, and ensure the same protection is applied to all related transmissions.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Communications between FPAC CASP / H2A and DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov occur using HTTPS.
mitigations.rationale: HTTPS reduces the likelihood of interception or disclosure while information is transmitted.

mitigations.description: Limit the pass-through entry point to only the minimum functions needed to route users to DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov, and avoid storing any additional user data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: FPAC CASP / H2A is used as a ‘pass through’ system to allow farmers and producers to access DOL and USCIS from a single (common) entry point.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing the functionality and data handled by the entry point lowers the privacy impact of a compromise.

mitigations.description: Keep the DOL case number retention strictly limited to the stated 90-day period and delete it promptly afterward.
mitigations.evidence_quote: This DOL case number is retained in FAPC CASP for 90 days.
mitigations.rationale: Shorter retention reduces the time during which the case number could be misused or linked to a user.

mitigations.description: Provide clear notice that data is transmitted to DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov and that FPAC CASP does not assess or perform actions on the data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: FPAC CASP / H2A does not assess or perform any actions on the data.
mitigations.rationale: Clear notice helps users understand how their information is handled once it leaves the system.

risks.description: The system stores highly sensitive PII, including SSNs, tax IDs, bank account details, and employment or producer records, which increases the harm if the data are misused or exposed. DRMS and TeamMate+ both contain records that can identify individuals and reveal financial or operational details.
risks.evidence_quote: Potential PII found in the encrypted documents includes: Name, Legal Name, Address, Tax ID number (individual or business), SSN, Data Universal Numbering System (DUNS) number, Registration in Central Contractor Registration database, Legal description of farm location, Tract Number, Deeds, Farm Shareholder salaries, Location, Farm ownership detail, Bank routing numbers, Deposit Account numbers, Contract numbers, Vendor ID.
risks.rationale: The presence of multiple high-impact identifiers and financial details raises the privacy impact of any unauthorized access or disclosure.

risks.description: Broad internal access and search capabilities could expose records to more staff than necessary if role restrictions are misapplied or too permissive. DRMS allows all staff to upload and search documents, and specialized roles can perform unconstrained searching for certain purposes.
risks.evidence_quote: All staff are able to upload and search for documents, limited by their organizational role and rights. Specialized roles for records managers and legal staff allow for lifecycle management of records or unconstrained searching for audit, legal discover, litigation holds, or Freedom Of Information Act inquiries.
risks.rationale: Wide search capability increases the chance that staff can view records beyond what is needed for their duties.

risks.description: The system's support for audit, legal discovery, litigation holds, and FOIA inquiries creates a risk that personal information will be disclosed more broadly than the individual expects. Those functions can surface records for non-routine purposes and may expose sensitive content in responses or reviews.
risks.evidence_quote: Specialized roles for records managers and legal staff allow for lifecycle management of records or unconstrained searching for audit, legal discover, litigation holds, or Freedom Of Information Act inquiries.
risks.rationale: Secondary uses like discovery and FOIA can expand access to personal data beyond ordinary business use.

risks.description: Contractor access introduces additional privacy risk because non-federal personnel may handle sensitive records. The system states that contractors will have access as part of their assigned duties.
risks.evidence_quote: Department contractors with a need-to-know will have access to Pipeline FPAC Mod as part of their regular assigned duties.
risks.rationale: Adding contractors increases the number of people who can access PII and the chance of improper handling.

risks.description: Administrator access, even though limited, concentrates powerful privileges in a small number of people and could allow broad exposure if misused. TeamMate+ administrators can access the application remotely and local access may be possible for administrative and configuration purposes.
risks.evidence_quote: Administrators, access to the TeamMate Plus application is restricted to 5 number of people. Administrator access can only be achieved by remote access and requires PIV or eAuth credentials authentication. Local access is restricted to remote access/console login for administrative and configuration purposes possible (if configured that way) made due to this application server being in the AWS datacenter.
risks.rationale: Privileged accounts can bypass ordinary user limitations, so misuse or compromise would have outsized privacy impact.

risks.description: The long retention period, including records kept indefinitely, increases the chance that personal data will remain available long after it is needed. DRMS and TeamMate+ retain information under NARA schedules and most applications may be retained permanently.
risks.evidence_quote: Information on most applications is retained indefinitely (permanent records).
risks.rationale: Longer retention extends the window in which records can be accessed, disclosed, or repurposed.

risks.description: TeamMate+ contains audit documentation about programs, controls, and errors that can implicate individuals or entities in improper payments, contracts, agreements, or eligibility determinations. If those records are mishandled, they could reveal sensitive findings about specific people or organizations.
risks.evidence_quote: The data are used in the FPAC financial audit process and serve as proof/documentation of findings. Audits are completed to identify program and administrative controls that are not adequate and allow for errors to be made. These errors can result in improper payments, contracts and agreements as well as ineligible producers that were deemed eligible, etc.,
risks.rationale: Audit findings can be sensitive because they document mistakes, eligibility issues, and financial consequences tied to identifiable subjects.

mitigations.description: Continue to enforce encryption for the stored documents and limit access to the minimum necessary users with need-to-know rights.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Potential PII found in the encrypted documents includes: Name, Legal Name, Address, Tax ID number (individual or business), SSN, Data Universal Numbering System (DUNS) number, Registration in Central Contractor Registration database, Legal description of farm location, Tract Number, Deeds, Farm Shareholder salaries, Location, Farm ownership detail, Bank routing numbers, Deposit Account numbers, Contract numbers, Vendor ID.
mitigations.rationale: Encrypting sensitive records and minimizing access reduces the impact of any unauthorized access.

mitigations.description: Tighten role-based access controls so staff can only upload and search the records needed for their official duties, and periodically review those roles and rights.
mitigations.evidence_quote: All staff are able to upload and search for documents, limited by their organizational role and rights.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting search and upload privileges lowers the chance of unnecessary internal exposure.

mitigations.description: Apply additional approval and logging controls for records used in legal discovery, litigation holds, and FOIA requests, and limit unconstrained searching to authorized records managers and legal staff only.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Specialized roles for records managers and legal staff allow for lifecycle management of records or unconstrained searching for audit, legal discover, litigation holds, or Freedom Of Information Act inquiries.
mitigations.rationale: Extra controls around secondary-use searches and disclosures help ensure personal data is only exposed when justified.

mitigations.description: Require contractors to receive the same need-to-know access review, training, and oversight as federal staff before they are granted access.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Department contractors with a need-to-know will have access to Pipeline FPAC Mod as part of their regular assigned duties.
mitigations.rationale: Contractor oversight reduces the risk that non-federal users mishandle sensitive records.

mitigations.description: Keep administrator access restricted to the smallest possible number of approved users and monitor remote administrative activity closely.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Administrators, access to the TeamMate Plus application is restricted to 5 number of people. Administrator access can only be achieved by remote access and requires PIV or eAuth credentials authentication.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting and monitoring privileged access reduces the likelihood of broad misuse of sensitive data.

mitigations.description: Regularly review retention schedules and delete or archive records in line with the approved NARA schedule rather than keeping data longer than necessary.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Information on most applications is retained indefinitely (permanent records).
mitigations.rationale: Shortening retention where allowed reduces the amount of personal data exposed over time.

mitigations.description: Limit access to audit reports and supporting records to authorized audit personnel and apply redaction where possible before sharing findings with customers or other stakeholders.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The data are used in the FPAC financial audit process and serve as proof/documentation of findings.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting and redacting audit materials helps protect sensitive information tied to findings.

risks.description: The system holds highly sensitive personal identifiers, including SSNs and EINs, which creates a risk of harm if the data is exposed or misused.
risks.evidence_quote: Name, Address, Phone Numbers, SSN, EIN number, eAuth JD/Name, Farm IDs
risks.rationale: SSNs and EINs are sensitive identifiers, so exposure would create significant privacy and identity-related harm.

risks.description: The system appears to collect and use data about multiple classes of people, including producers, agents, loss adjusters, employees, affiliates, and other persons, increasing the scope of privacy impact.
risks.evidence_quote: This data is being collected to determine the eligibility of producers, agents and loss adjusters for the Federal Crop Insurance Program
risks.rationale: Broader categories of data subjects increase the number of people affected by any privacy failure.

risks.description: Internal sharing for forensic data mining could expose PII beyond the original operational need and create secondary-use privacy risk.
risks.evidence_quote: The data is primarily shared with the RMA Strategic Data Analysis Division. This group performs the forensic data mining of RMA's data, looking for indications of Fraud, Waste, and Abuse.
risks.rationale: Using operational PII for fraud analysis expands access and increases the chance of overcollection or misuse.

risks.description: External sharing with Approved Insurance Providers creates a disclosure risk because PII leaves USDA and is handled by outside entities.
risks.evidence_quote: Policy information is shared only with the Approved insurance Providers (AIP). These are the very entities that collect the information.
risks.rationale: Any external disclosure increases the risk of unauthorized access or mishandling outside the agency.

risks.description: The system transmits PII over network connections, so interception or compromise during transfer is a privacy risk.
risks.evidence_quote: The data is transmitted via a dedicated VPN line
risks.rationale: Even protected network transmission can be targeted or misconfigured, creating disclosure risk in transit.

risks.description: Contractor access to the system increases the risk of unauthorized viewing or misuse of PII.
risks.evidence_quote: 8.2 Will Department contractors have access to the system? Yes
risks.rationale: Additional users with access increase the attack surface and the chance of inappropriate access.

risks.description: Retaining most application records indefinitely increases the risk that PII will be kept longer than necessary and remain vulnerable over time.
risks.evidence_quote: Information on most applications is retained indefinitely (permanent records).
risks.rationale: Long retention extends the period during which data can be exposed, breached, or repurposed.

risks.description: The system uses hard copy forms and e-forms, which creates a risk of collection or handling errors that could affect privacy and accuracy.
risks.evidence_quote: The information is collected via hard copy forms and e-forms completed by the insured producer, insurance agent, or adjustor.
risks.rationale: Manual and form-based collection can lead to misentry, loss, or unauthorized viewing of PII.

mitigations.description: Limit access to SSNs and EINs to only the roles that must use them, and require protection of those identifiers in accordance with Privacy Act requirements.
mitigations.evidence_quote: SSNs or EINs shall be protected, as prescribed in the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 USC § 552a), by the Company and all of its affiliates with access to such information.
mitigations.rationale: Role-based protection reduces the chance that highly sensitive identifiers are exposed unnecessarily.

mitigations.description: Restrict fraud-analysis access to the minimum data needed and audit the RMA Strategic Data Analysis Division's use of the data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The data is primarily shared with the RMA Strategic Data Analysis Division. This group performs the forensic data mining of RMA's data, looking for indications of Fraud, Waste, and Abuse.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting and auditing secondary use reduces the privacy impact of forensic analysis.

mitigations.description: Continue to share only the information collected by the AIPs and require the external recipients to follow the published SORN and Privacy Act protections.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, this information is only shared with the AIPs that collected the information. Collection of data is conducted in accordance with the published SORN.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting external disclosure to the collecting entity narrows the privacy exposure.

mitigations.description: Keep using encrypted VPN transmission for all external disclosures and dedicated VPN lines for internal sharing.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The data is transmitted via a dedicated VPN line
mitigations.rationale: Encrypted network transport helps protect PII from interception in transit.

mitigations.description: Apply the same identification and access controls to contractors as to RMA staff, and review contractor access regularly.
mitigations.evidence_quote: AIP access is controlled via the same 586 identification process as used by RMA.
mitigations.rationale: Consistent access controls help prevent unauthorized access by non-employee users.

mitigations.description: Retain records only for the applicable NARA schedule and periodically review whether any application truly needs permanent retention.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The archiving and retention strategy for applications on Pipeline RMA HVA will be retained in accordance with the NARA Retention Schedule.
mitigations.rationale: Periodic retention review reduces unnecessary long-term exposure of PII.

mitigations.description: Use validation and edit checks on submitted policy data to reduce collection and entry errors.
mitigations.evidence_quote: PASS contains processes that edit and validate detail policy data submitted by the approved insurance providers to provide reasonable assurance that the data is accurate and timely
mitigations.rationale: Validation helps prevent inaccurate or mishandled PII from entering the system.

risks.description: The CFPB may collect identifying information from people who interact with it on social media, creating a privacy risk if that PII is not expected by the user. This includes information such as names, usernames, email addresses, IP addresses, geographic information, or demographic information.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may collect or use a limited amount of Personally Identifiable Information (“PII”) when using social media to further its ability to interact with the public. PII is any information that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual’s identity such as name, username, email address, Internet Protocol (IP) address, geographic information, or demographic information.
risks.rationale: Collecting identifiable data from public interactions can expose individuals to privacy harm if they do not anticipate what is being collected.

risks.description: Social media interactions may expose personal information to third-party platform operators, creating a risk that data is handled outside CFPB-controlled systems. The platforms themselves are not government systems and may apply their own collection and use practices.
risks.evidence_quote: Social media platforms are generally controlled and operated by non-government third parties.
risks.rationale: When a third party controls the platform, users' information can be subject to handling beyond CFPB's direct control.

risks.description: People may not fully understand when their information is being collected or used through social media, which can undermine informed participation. The system context acknowledges that social media use raises privacy concerns and that the public expects protections.
risks.evidence_quote: Use of social media raises concerns related to the protection of personal privacy. The CFPB understands that the public expects certain privacy protections when interacting with the Bureau through social media.
risks.rationale: If users do not have clear notice, they may share information without understanding the privacy implications.

risks.description: Although the CFPB says it does not use the information to make determinations about individuals, any collected PII could still be retained or reused in ways that create privacy exposure if controls fail. This risk is heightened because the system is intended to engage the public broadly, not just a narrow set of known users.
risks.evidence_quote: Does the CFPB use the information to benefit or make a determination about an individual? No.
risks.rationale: Even without formal determinations, retained identifying data can still be misused or exposed if not tightly controlled.

mitigations.description: Limit collection of PII to the smallest amount needed for the social media interaction and avoid collecting unnecessary identifying details.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB may collect or use a limited amount of Personally Identifiable Information (“PII”) when using social media to further its ability to interact with the public.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing collection reduces the amount of sensitive identifying information at risk.

mitigations.description: Apply standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls to any PII collected through social media.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Using established controls helps reduce the chance of unauthorized handling or exposure.

mitigations.description: Provide clear notice to users about what information may be collected and how it will be used when they interact with CFPB on social media.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
mitigations.rationale: Clear notice supports informed participation and reduces surprise collection.

mitigations.description: Ensure the collected information is covered by the applicable system of records notice and is handled only for the stated public-engagement purpose.
mitigations.evidence_quote: To the extent that the CFPB may collect PII through social media interactions, this information would be covered by the Social Networks and Citizen Engagement System (CFPB.006) System of Records Notice.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting use to the stated records system and purpose reduces the risk of inappropriate reuse.

risks.description: The system makes agency staff contact details broadly public, which can expose names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, and websites of individuals associated with HUD-approved housing counseling agencies. This creates a risk of unwanted contact, spam, or other privacy harms to those individuals.
risks.evidence_quote: HUD makes this information available to the public.
risks.rationale: Public disclosure of personally identifying contact information increases exposure of the affected individuals.

risks.description: Users of the locator tool are identified at least by ZIP code, and that ZIP code is collected and retained with tool analytics. Even though it is limited, a ZIP code can still reveal approximate location and support profiling of a user's housing-related interests.
risks.evidence_quote: PII collected from users of the CFPB housing counselor locator tool includes:  ZIP code entered for search results.
risks.rationale: Location data can be sensitive when tied to a housing search.

risks.description: The system retains consumerfinance.gov user analytics and ZIP codes as permanent records until a disposition schedule is approved, which increases the chance of long-term secondary use or exposure beyond the original search purpose.
risks.evidence_quote: records collected through consumerfinance.gov (user analytics and ZIP codes entered in the locator tool) are being managed as permanent records until the disposition schedule for these records is approved by the National Archives and Records Administration
risks.rationale: Long retention expands the window for misuse, breach, or repurposing.

risks.description: The public API and locator tool allow outside users and developers to retrieve and republish the dataset in other applications or formats, which can multiply disclosure and make downstream privacy controls harder to enforce. This increases the chance that the public data will be copied, combined with other data, or used in ways not anticipated by the original system.
risks.evidence_quote: The API, owned and managed by HUD, enables users to retrieve the HUD counselor dataset and use that data for their own applications or systems outside of CFPB.
risks.rationale: External redistribution makes it harder to control subsequent uses of the data.

risks.description: The tool is designed to return the ten closest counselors for a ZIP code, and users can query or download data in multiple formats. Repeated or targeted queries could still be used to infer more about a person's location or search intent than intended.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB housing counselor locator tool permits users to query the HUD counselor dataset to return the ten closest counselors.
risks.rationale: Search functionality can reveal user intent and approximate location through repeated use.

risks.description: The system collects non-identifying browser and usage details for functionality, security, and usability evaluation, which can still create behavioral profiles when combined over time. This may allow tracking of how individuals use the site even if the data are not directly identifying.
risks.evidence_quote: consumerfinance.gov collects other non‐identifying information from users of the CFPB housing counselor locator tool as part of normal operations supporting website functionality and security, (e.g. visit timestamps, browser version and operating system, pages viewed and time on site, etc.)
risks.rationale: Usage metadata can become privacy-sensitive when accumulated and analyzed.

mitigations.description: Limit public disclosure to the minimum contact information needed for the locator function and keep the dataset restricted to the already public agency information.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB is republishing this publicly available data on its website and creating a tool by which users can more easily search the dataset in order to locate HUD‐approved housing counseling agencies in their area.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing exposed fields reduces unnecessary personal contact disclosure.

mitigations.description: Collect only the ZIP code needed to return search results and avoid retaining it beyond the search session unless strictly needed for a documented purpose.
mitigations.evidence_quote: ZIP codes entered by users of the locator tool are collected in order to provide users with a list of HUD‐approved housing counseling agencies within a specified range of their input ZIP code.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting collection and retention reduces location privacy risk.

mitigations.description: Approve and implement a NARA disposition schedule as soon as possible, and dispose of consumerfinance.gov ZIP codes and analytics according to that schedule.
mitigations.evidence_quote: records collected through consumerfinance.gov (user analytics and ZIP codes entered in the locator tool) are being managed as permanent records until the disposition schedule for these records is approved by the National Archives and Records Administration, at which time, the CFPB will dispose of such files in accordance with the schedule.
mitigations.rationale: A formal disposal schedule shortens retention and lowers long-term exposure.

mitigations.description: Publish clear downstream-use terms and technical guidance for API users to discourage republishing beyond the intended public dataset and to support consistent privacy handling in external applications.
mitigations.rationale: Guidance can reduce uncontrolled downstream copying and misuse of the public API data.

mitigations.description: Continue limiting locator results to the ten closest counselors and avoid exposing any more precise record-level search capability through the public interface.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The locator tool is programmed to always return the ten closest results, meaning users may not isolate a single record using the tool.
mitigations.rationale: Coarse results reduce the chance of pinpointing a specific record or person.

mitigations.description: Minimize analytics collection to what is necessary for functionality, security, and usability evaluation, and aggregate or de-identify usage data before analysis where possible.
mitigations.evidence_quote: consumerfinance.gov collects other non‐identifying information from users of the CFPB housing counselor locator tool as part of normal operations supporting website functionality and security, (e.g. visit timestamps, browser version and operating system, pages viewed and time on site, etc.)
mitigations.rationale: Reducing detail in usage logs lowers the chance of behavioral tracking.

risks.description: The system can expose highly sensitive personal information, including financial account numbers, biometric information, and health or medical information, if it is mishandled or disclosed improperly.
risks.evidence_quote: Project/System includes information about: Federal Employees Contractors Consultants The Public ... Other Information (including biometric information and health or medical information)
risks.rationale: Sensitive data increases the harm if access is not tightly controlled or if disclosure occurs.

risks.description: Matching records across datasets and using unique record locators can create richer profiles and enable linkage of data about individuals from multiple sources.
risks.evidence_quote: Market Research may involve the matching of records across different datasets. For example, the CFPB may obtain updates or supplements to a dataset and, in those circumstances, may use record locators unique to the entity providing the update in order to update or supplement the individual records.
risks.rationale: Cross-dataset matching increases the risk of re-identification and unintended secondary use.

risks.description: The system may collect direct identifiers such as name, phone number, home address, email, and financial account number, which can directly identify individuals if retained or shared.
risks.evidence_quote: In certain circumstances, Administrative Data collected for Market Research may include direct identifying PII, including: • Name • Phone number • Home address • Email • Financial account number
risks.rationale: Direct identifiers make it easier to identify and contact individuals and increase disclosure risk.

risks.description: Administrative data is collected from third parties, commercial sources, and public databases without direct collection from consumers, so individuals may not know their information is being used for Market Research.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB collects Administrative Data only from third parties, commercial sources and public databases, not directly from consumers
risks.rationale: Lack of direct collection can reduce transparency and limit individuals' ability to understand or contest use of their data.

risks.description: The CFPB retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a records disposition schedule, which can prolong exposure and increase the amount of data held over time.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Long retention increases the window for unauthorized access, breach, or stale data use.

risks.description: The system may share research results with the general public, the source of the administrative data, and federal financial regulators, creating a disclosure risk if outputs are not adequately aggregated.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share the results of Market Research with the general public, the source of the Administrative Data, and/or federal financial regulators.
risks.rationale: Sharing outputs more broadly can reveal sensitive patterns even when direct identifiers are removed.

risks.description: Because the system includes race/ethnicity, gender, age, education level, and income, analyses could reveal sensitive demographic patterns about individuals or small groups.
risks.evidence_quote: Demographic information, such as race/ethnicity, gender, age, education level, and income
risks.rationale: Demographic attributes can be sensitive and can enable discrimination or stigmatization if exposed.

risks.description: Only CFPB personnel with a need to know can access the data, but the presence of internal access still creates an insider misuse or unauthorized access risk.
risks.evidence_quote: Only CFPB personnel with a need to know are granted access to Administrative Data used for Market Research.
risks.rationale: Any internal access path can be abused or misused without strong controls and monitoring.

mitigations.description: Restrict access to sensitive fields and apply strict disclosure controls before any use or sharing of data containing biometric, health, or financial account information.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Only CFPB personnel with a need to know are granted access to Administrative Data used for Market Research.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting access to sensitive data reduces the chance of improper disclosure.

mitigations.description: Minimize cross-dataset matching and use de-identified copies for research and analysis after matching is complete.
mitigations.evidence_quote: After the matching is complete, a de-identified copy of the matched dataset will be used for conducting research and analysis.
mitigations.rationale: Using de-identified copies after linkage lowers the risk of ongoing re-identification.

mitigations.description: Remove direct identifiers whenever they are not necessary and keep only stripped or de-identified data for analysis.
mitigations.evidence_quote: At times, the Bureau will analyze account-, loan-, or transaction- level data stripped of direct identifying PII.
mitigations.rationale: Stripping direct identifiers reduces the likelihood that records can be tied back to individuals.

mitigations.description: Provide notice through the third parties, commercial sources, or public databases that supply the data, and document when notice is required.
mitigations.evidence_quote: it is those third parties’ responsibility to determine whether notice is required and to provide any requisite notice.
mitigations.rationale: Notice improves transparency for individuals whose data is used without direct collection.

mitigations.description: Adopt and obtain approval for a records disposition schedule as soon as possible and dispose of records according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Records that fall under a general records schedule will be disposed of according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.rationale: A defined retention schedule reduces unnecessary long-term exposure.

mitigations.description: Ensure all public or external research outputs are aggregated and do not include direct identifying information.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Products of Market Research consist of aggregate information, such as tabulations and statistical results, that are included in internal reports, CFPB whitepapers and studies, and other policy output, and do not contain direct identifying PII.
mitigations.rationale: Aggregation lowers the chance that shared results identify individuals.

mitigations.description: Apply disclosure review to demographic outputs so that small-cell or otherwise sensitive demographic information is not released in a way that identifies people.
mitigations.rationale: Sensitive demographic data can still be revealing even when direct identifiers are removed.

mitigations.description: Maintain need-to-know access controls and review access authorization regularly for personnel handling Market Research data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Only CFPB personnel with a need to know are granted access to Administrative Data used for Market Research.
mitigations.rationale: Regular access review helps prevent unnecessary internal exposure.

risks.description: People may be re-identified by combining the loan-level fields with other public or private data, even though the dataset lacks direct identifiers. The combination of application year, loan amount, action taken, denial reason, geography, and property type can still point to a specific borrower or household in a small area.
risks.evidence_quote: The HMDA Public Use Dataset does not include any information that directly identifies an individual. The HMDA Public Use Dataset includes the following information: • Loan data o Application year o Loan or application type, purpose, amount (rounded to nearest thousand) o Action taken and denial reason, if applicable o HOEPA flag o Lien status (first, subordinate, unsecured) o Rate spread on higher-priced mortgages o Purchaser type o Preapproval request • Property data o Census tract, Metropolitan Statistical Area or Metropolitan Division, State, County o Property type
risks.rationale: Detailed quasi-identifiers can make a record unique enough to link back to a person or household.

risks.description: Sensitive inferences about financial status or credit decisions can be drawn from the public dataset. Fields such as denial reason, rate spread, lien status, and loan amount can reveal information about a person's borrowing history and financial circumstances.
risks.evidence_quote: The HMDA Public Use Dataset includes the following information: • Loan data o Application year o Loan or application type, purpose, amount (rounded to nearest thousand) o Action taken and denial reason, if applicable o HOEPA flag o Lien status (first, subordinate, unsecured) o Rate spread on higher-priced mortgages o Purchaser type o Preapproval request
risks.rationale: Even without names, the data can expose sensitive financial attributes about an individual loan applicant.

risks.description: The public availability of the dataset creates broad downstream sharing and reuse risk, including by private-sector organizations and agencies that may combine it with other datasets. Once users can download or share the data in multiple formats, the CFPB has limited control over subsequent privacy-preserving use.
risks.evidence_quote: The data publishing API also enables users to download or share data in the Dataset in a variety of formats.
risks.rationale: Open distribution increases the chance that others will repurpose the data in ways that reduce privacy protections.

risks.description: Because users can query and filter the dataset and may isolate a single record, a record-level disclosure risk remains even without direct identifiers. A user could focus on a very small set of transactions and infer the identity of the borrower from context.
risks.evidence_quote: Users may be able to isolate a single record, but the record will not contain any direct identifiers.
risks.rationale: Single-record outputs are easier to match to an individual through external knowledge.

risks.description: The system relies on upstream redaction to protect applicant and borrower privacy, but the CFPB does not independently verify the accuracy or completeness of the republished dataset before making it public. If redaction is incomplete or incorrect, privacy-sensitive fields could be exposed.
risks.evidence_quote: The regulators redact certain fields for the purpose of protecting applicant and borrower privacy and then share it with the public on the FFIEC website.
risks.rationale: Privacy protection depends on correct upstream masking, so errors there can leak data.

risks.description: The dataset may remain available longer than intended because the CFPB will keep it until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA. Extended retention increases the time window for re-identification and misuse.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB will continue to retain these records until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA.
risks.rationale: Longer retention extends exposure and the opportunity for misuse over time.

mitigations.description: Continue and strengthen field suppression, rounding, and geographic/generalization controls before publication so that records are less likely to be unique.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The information reported to regulators pursuant to HMDA and Regulation C is modified to protect loan applicant privacy and is made available to the public annually on the FFIEC’s website.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing quasi-identifiers lowers the chance that a record can be linked back to a person.

mitigations.description: Limit the granularity of sensitive loan attributes in public outputs, especially where denial reasons, rate spread, or exact geography are not needed for the public purpose.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The HMDA Public Use Dataset includes the following information: • Loan data o Application year o Loan or application type, purpose, amount (rounded to nearest thousand) o Action taken and denial reason, if applicable o HOEPA flag o Lien status (first, subordinate, unsecured) o Rate spread on higher-priced mortgages o Purchaser type o Preapproval request
mitigations.rationale: Less granular sensitive fields reduce the amount of personal financial inference available to users.

mitigations.description: Publish clear reuse guidance and privacy warnings alongside downloads and API access to discourage attempts to re-identify individuals or combine the data with other sources.
mitigations.rationale: User-facing restrictions and warnings can reduce harmful downstream reuse even when the dataset is public.

mitigations.description: Apply query result thresholds or suppress outputs that would return very small cell counts or a single record when users filter the API or generate tables.
mitigations.rationale: Preventing tiny outputs makes it harder to isolate a borrower from the public data.

mitigations.description: Add an independent privacy review or quality-control step before republication to check that upstream redaction remains effective and that no direct identifiers or overly specific fields are present.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB accepts the HMDA Public Use Dataset from the FFIEC as accurate and complete, and does not alter the data or independently verify the accuracy and completeness of the dataset before republishing it on consumerfinance.gov.
mitigations.rationale: Independent review can catch masking failures before the dataset is exposed publicly.

mitigations.description: Adopt and publish a NARA-approved retention schedule as soon as possible, and remove or archive the dataset according to that schedule.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The HMDA Public Use Dataset is currently retained in accordance with the Federal Reserve Board Schedule N1-082-05-1, Home Mortgage Disclosure Act and Related Records. The CFPB will continue to retain these records until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA.
mitigations.rationale: A formal retention limit reduces the duration of public exposure.

risks.description: Direct identifiers and sensitive personal data could be exposed if they are not fully separated from research data or are accessed by people who do not need them. The system collects names, contact details, SSNs, and other sensitive information, including health and biometric information.
risks.evidence_quote: PROJECT/SYSTEM INCLUDES: Name and other biographic information (e.g. date of birth) Contact Information (address, zip code, telephone number, email address) Social Security number (“SSN”) or other identifier Financial Information User and Online Information Third Party Information Other Information (including biometric information and health or medical information)
risks.rationale: Collecting highly sensitive identifiers increases the harm if the data is improperly accessed or disclosed.

risks.description: Record matching can create new combined profiles that increase re-identification and inference risk. The system may match credit score and other administrative data to response data, creating new assemblies of information about respondents.
risks.evidence_quote: In some cases, Consumer Experience Research may involve the matching of records, such as credit score to Response Data, creating new assemblies of information about the Respondent.
risks.rationale: Linking datasets can make individuals easier to identify and reveal more about them than any single dataset alone.

risks.description: Public or external research outputs could still reveal individuals if disclosure protections fail or if direct identifiers are included in case studies or quotes. The system disseminates research results to the general public and sometimes seeks to share direct identifying PII in external products.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share products of Consumer Experience Research externally, including by disseminating research results to the general public.
risks.rationale: External publication broadens exposure and can create privacy harm if de-identification is incomplete.

risks.description: Third-party and contractor handling of data increases the risk of unauthorized access or disclosure during transfers and collaboration. The system uses contractor systems, vendor websites, encrypted email, and collaborations with other researchers.
risks.evidence_quote: Most systems, such as contractor systems supporting Consumer Experience Research, are not directly integrated with any other CFPB system. Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated data transfers between contractor systems and/or vendor websites and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels.
risks.rationale: More organizations and transfer points generally increase the chance of mishandling or unauthorized disclosure.

risks.description: Administrative data may be used to identify survey recipients or analyze nonresponse, which could expose people to contact they did not expect or to profiling based on third-party records. The system uses third-party administrative data to identify potential recipients of surveys and to support nonresponse analyses.
risks.evidence_quote: In some instances, the CFPB may use Administrative Data collected from a third party to identify potential recipients of surveys, to provide auxiliary information for research, and to support nonresponse analyses.
risks.rationale: Using third-party data for targeting or analysis can affect privacy expectations and create unwanted inference about individuals.

risks.description: Indefinite retention of computer and paper records increases the long-term risk of misuse, breach, or secondary use beyond the original research purpose. The system keeps records until NARA approves a disposition schedule.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: The longer sensitive records are kept, the longer they remain exposed to potential loss or misuse.

mitigations.description: Store direct identifying PII separately from research data and limit access to personnel with a need to know.
mitigations.evidence_quote: When direct identifying PII is necessary to facilitate Consumer Experience Research rather than necessary to the analysis, the direct identifying PII is stored and secured separately.
mitigations.rationale: Separating identifiers from analytic data reduces the chance that sensitive information is exposed unnecessarily.

mitigations.description: Use de-identified copies of matched datasets for analysis after matching is complete.
mitigations.evidence_quote: After the matching is complete, a de- identified copy of the matched dataset is used for conducting research and analysis.
mitigations.rationale: Removing direct identifiers after linkage lowers the risk that combined records can be tied back to individuals.

mitigations.description: Apply disclosure-protection procedures to all external products, including aggregation, rounding, exclusion of some variables, and exclusion of observations, and obtain consent before sharing direct identifying PII.
mitigations.evidence_quote: These external products are subject to disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation of response categories, rounding, exclusion of some variables, or exclusion of observations, and typically do not include direct identifying PII. If the CPFB seeks to share direct identifying PII in an external product, it will obtain consent of the appropriate Respondents prior to disclosure.
mitigations.rationale: These steps reduce the chance that published outputs can identify respondents.

mitigations.description: Use encrypted tunnels for transfers and legal agreements and non-disclosure agreements for external collaborators.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated data transfers between contractor systems and/or vendor websites and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels.
mitigations.rationale: Encryption and contractual restrictions help limit unauthorized access during transfer and collaboration.

mitigations.description: Collect and use third-party administrative data only with consent where required and use it only for the stated research functions.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Consumer Experience Research primarily relies on information collected directly from the individual and subject to the individual’s consent for the CFPB to collect additional information from third parties
mitigations.rationale: Consent and purpose limitation reduce the privacy impact of using third-party records for targeting and analysis.

mitigations.description: Dispose of records according to an approved records schedule as soon as one exists, rather than retaining them indefinitely.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Records that fall under a general records schedule will be disposed of according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.rationale: Timely disposal limits the period during which sensitive records remain exposed.

risks.description: Individuals may not know their information was collected or how it will be used or disclosed, reducing transparency and limiting their ability to understand or contest the handling of their data.
risks.evidence_quote: individuals generally will not receive notice that the information is being requested and therefore how such information will be used or disclosed.
risks.rationale: The system explicitly says notice generally is not provided for supervisory or enforcement collection.

risks.description: Matching records across datasets can create a more detailed profile of a person and increase the chance of reidentification or unintended linkage, even when direct identifiers are stripped.
risks.evidence_quote: Use of SEFL Data for Market Research may involve the matching of records across different datasets.
risks.rationale: Cross-dataset matching increases linkage risk because the system combines information from multiple sources.

risks.description: The system may handle highly sensitive direct identifiers and financial details, so unauthorized access or disclosure could expose personal and financial information.
risks.evidence_quote: In most cases, SEFL Data used for Market Research will not contain direct identifying PII. However, in some cases they may include direct identifying PII, including: • Name • Phone number • Home address • Email • Financial account number • Social Security number
risks.rationale: The presence of direct identifiers and account data raises the impact of any disclosure.

risks.description: Sharing information under routine uses or with external recipients can expose data beyond the original collection context, creating secondary use and disclosure risk.
risks.evidence_quote: the CFPB may share information as outlined in the Routine Uses of each applicable SORN.
risks.rationale: Routine-use sharing expands the number of parties that may receive the information.

risks.description: Indefinite retention of computer and paper records increases the risk that personal data will be kept longer than necessary and be available for future misuse or breach.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Long retention extends exposure time and can preserve data beyond immediate operational need.

risks.description: Using direct identifying PII to contact potential survey recipients could reveal that a person is associated with a supervisory, enforcement, or market research inquiry.
risks.evidence_quote: When the CFPB does use direct identifying PII in analyses, it does so in order to a) match across datasets; b) update data sets; and c) contact potential recipients of surveys
risks.rationale: Contacting people based on these records can disclose their connection to CFPB activity.

mitigations.description: Provide direct notice to individuals whenever feasible before collecting or sharing their information, and clearly explain the collection, use, and disclosure practices.
mitigations.evidence_quote: In cases where notice cannot be provided or is not required, the CFPB has provided constructive notice of how it may use such information through this PIA.
mitigations.rationale: The PIA already relies on constructive notice, so direct notice would better address the transparency gap when feasible.

mitigations.description: Limit record matching to the minimum necessary fields and use de-identified copies for analysis after matching is complete.
mitigations.evidence_quote: After the matching is complete, a de-identified copy of the matched dataset is used for conducting Market Research and analysis.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing identifiers and analyzing de-identified copies reduces linkage and reidentification risk.

mitigations.description: Restrict direct identifying PII to narrowly necessary uses and keep access limited to personnel with a need to know.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Only CFPB personnel with a need to know are granted access to SEFL Data used for Market Research.
mitigations.rationale: Need-to-know access reduces the chance that sensitive identifiers are exposed unnecessarily.

mitigations.description: Apply disclosure controls before any sharing and continue to limit external release to aggregate products that do not directly identify individuals.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share the products of Market Research with the general public and federal financial regulators. Any such results do not include information that directly identifies any individual.
mitigations.rationale: Sharing only aggregate, non-identifying outputs reduces secondary disclosure risk.

mitigations.description: Finalize and follow a NARA-approved records disposition schedule as soon as possible, and dispose of records according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Records that fall under a general records schedule will be disposed of according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.rationale: A disposition schedule limits how long personal data remain exposed in the system.

mitigations.description: Use survey contact only when necessary and separate contact information from research datasets after outreach is complete.
mitigations.rationale: Separating outreach data from research data reduces the chance that a person’s identity is linked to CFPB research activity.

risks.description: The system can collect and store direct identifiers together with response, administrative, and demographic data, creating a re-identification risk if datasets are linked or mishandled. This is especially sensitive because the system may include financial, health, and biometric information.
risks.evidence_quote: The Bureau may use the following direct identifying PII to facilitate and administer Consumer Education: • Names • Phone Number • Email Address • Mailing Address ... Consumer Education may be associated with Administrative Data ... • Balances and credit line limits
risks.rationale: Combining identifiers with detailed consumer data increases the chance that individuals can be singled out or re-identified.

risks.description: The system may create new information about participants through record matching, including linking credit score or administrative data to response data. That creates a risk that sensitive inferences are generated and retained beyond what participants expect.
risks.evidence_quote: In some special cases, Consumer Education may involve the matching of records, such as credit score to Response Data, creating new information about the Participant.
risks.rationale: Record linkage can reveal more about a person than any single dataset alone.

risks.description: Although the system says matching is subject to informed consent, participants may still face privacy loss if consent is not sufficiently informed or if matching is broader than they understand. This is a risk because the system uses personal and administrative data for analysis after matching.
risks.evidence_quote: Such matching is only conducted subject to the Participant’s informed consent.
risks.rationale: Consent reduces but does not eliminate the risk that participants do not fully understand the downstream use of their data.

risks.description: The system shares response data in some cases and may share products with the general public, which could expose participant information if aggregation or disclosure protections are insufficient. Even without direct identifiers, detailed categories or small groups could still be identifying.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may also share the products of Consumer Education or Response Data with the general public, but any products disclosed do not include direct identifying PII, and will typically be subject to further disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation of response categories, generalized sentiments of Participants, rounding, exclusion of some variables, or exclusion of observations.
risks.rationale: Public disclosure can still create re-identification or inference risk when data are detailed or sparse.

risks.description: The system may share response data with other recipients after providing notice, which creates a risk of secondary use beyond the original collection purpose. Participants may choose whether to participate, but the data can still be disclosed once shared.
risks.evidence_quote: When the CFPB does share Response Data, the CFPB provides notice to the Participants through the notice mechanisms discussed in Section 2.2, and Participants can then choose whether they want to participate given that sharing.
risks.rationale: Notice and choice help, but any downstream sharing increases the chance of broader use or exposure.

risks.description: Contractors, other federal agencies, and academic institutions may access the data, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse by collaborators. The system relies on legal agreements and nondisclosure agreements, which may not fully prevent improper access.
risks.evidence_quote: When the CFPB collaborates with other researchers, such as those at other federal agencies or academic institutions, legal agreements and non-disclosure agreements are used to restrict access to the data, as appropriate.
risks.rationale: External access expands the number of people and organizations that can handle sensitive data.

risks.description: Pushed, non-automated transfers via encrypted tunnels and encrypted email create a risk of transmission errors or accidental disclosure during data movement. Manual transfer processes can increase the chance that data are sent to the wrong place or handled inconsistently.
risks.evidence_quote: Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated transfers between contractor systems and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels. These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
risks.rationale: Manual transfer workflows are more error-prone than fully automated controls.

risks.description: The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a records disposition schedule, which increases the long-term risk of unauthorized access, breach, or reuse. Retaining records longer than necessary also increases the amount of data exposed if a compromise occurs.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until the National Archives and Records Administration (“NARA”) approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Longer retention generally increases the window of vulnerability and the potential impact of any incident.

risks.description: The system includes information about lower-income and vulnerable consumers, including disabled consumers, which creates a heightened sensitivity risk if their data are disclosed or misused. These populations may face greater harm from exposure of financial, demographic, or health-related information.
risks.evidence_quote: More narrow initiatives may focus on more specific populations, including: • Lower-income and vulnerable consumers, including disabled consumers;
risks.rationale: Sensitive populations can experience greater harm from privacy incidents than the general public.

mitigations.description: Keep direct identifying PII stored separately from response and administrative data, and limit collection to what is necessary for recruitment, scheduling, or comparison.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Direct identifying PII is separated from Participants’ Response Data and (where relevant) Administrative Data for the CFPB’s research purposes.
mitigations.rationale: Separation and minimization reduce the chance that linked datasets will identify individuals.

mitigations.description: Use de-identified copies of matched datasets for research and analysis after matching is complete.
mitigations.evidence_quote: After the matching is complete, a de-identified copy of the matched dataset is used for conducting research and analysis.
mitigations.rationale: Using de-identified outputs lowers the risk that analysts will see directly identifying linked records.

mitigations.description: Require documented informed consent that clearly explains any record matching and the kinds of data that may be linked before matching occurs.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Such matching is only conducted subject to the Participant’s informed consent.
mitigations.rationale: Clear consent helps ensure participants understand and accept the matching use of their data.

mitigations.description: Continue using disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation, generalized sentiments, rounding, exclusion of some variables, and exclusion of observations before any public release.
mitigations.evidence_quote: subject to further disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation of response categories, generalized sentiments of Participants, rounding, exclusion of some variables, or exclusion of observations.
mitigations.rationale: These techniques reduce the likelihood that public products can be traced back to a person.

mitigations.description: Provide notice to participants before any sharing of response data and allow them to choose whether to participate in that sharing.
mitigations.evidence_quote: the CFPB provides notice to the Participants through the notice mechanisms discussed in Section 2.2, and Participants can then choose whether they want to participate given that sharing.
mitigations.rationale: Notice and choice give participants control over whether their data are shared.

mitigations.description: Restrict collaborator access through legal agreements and nondisclosure agreements, and grant access only when appropriate.
mitigations.evidence_quote: legal agreements and non-disclosure agreements are used to restrict access to the data, as appropriate.
mitigations.rationale: Binding access restrictions help limit misuse by external collaborators.

mitigations.description: Continue using encrypted tunnels and an encrypted email client for system transfers, and add transfer verification checks for manual exchanges.
mitigations.evidence_quote: which take place via encrypted tunnels. These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
mitigations.rationale: Encryption protects data in transit, and verification checks would further reduce accidental disclosure during manual transfers.

mitigations.description: Adopt and obtain approval for a records disposition schedule as soon as possible, and dispose of records according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Records that fall under a general records schedule will be disposed of according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.rationale: Timely disposition shortens the period during which retained records can be exposed.

mitigations.description: Apply heightened access and disclosure controls to datasets involving vulnerable consumers, including tighter need-to-know review and stronger disclosure suppression before sharing.
mitigations.rationale: Additional controls are appropriate because the system serves populations that may face greater harm from disclosure.

risks.description: Primary data collection in the field may collect more personal information than is necessary for market research purposes.
risks.evidence_quote: As part of its research programs, the Bureau utilizes primary data collection in the consumer financial market (“Market Research in the Field”).
risks.rationale: Primary data collection in real-world settings can increase the amount of personal information gathered, which raises collection-minimization risk.

risks.description: Sharing research data with third-party collaborators can expose participant information to external organizations.
risks.evidence_quote: When conducting Market Research in the Field, the CFPB may collaborate with third parties, including consumer financial products or service providers, innovators, entrepreneurs, non- profit or academic institutions, community-based organizations, or nonprofits; and social science researchers who are active in or may contribute insight into the consumer financial market.
risks.rationale: Collaboration with outside entities creates a disclosure risk because data may flow beyond CFPB control.

risks.description: Using contractors or accepting third-party collaboration proposals can create accountability gaps if roles and responsibilities are not well controlled.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may lead Market Research in the Field directly, contract with a third party, or accept a collaboration proposal submitted by a third party.
risks.rationale: Multiple operating models increase the chance that privacy responsibilities are unclear or unevenly applied.

risks.description: Field research may involve longer-term observation of consumer behavior, increasing the chance of persistent tracking or profiling of participants.
risks.evidence_quote: Via Market Research in the Field, the CFPB can evaluate how economic activity operates in naturally occurring environments, and it generally allows for research to occur over a longer period of time than in a lab setting.
risks.rationale: Longer observation periods can reveal patterns about individuals over time, which heightens privacy sensitivity.

risks.description: The system may rely on notice and consent opportunities that are only generally applicable, which could leave participants insufficiently informed or in control.
risks.evidence_quote: Generally applicable: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
risks.rationale: General opportunities for notice and consent may not be specific enough to ensure meaningful participant understanding and choice.

risks.description: If access and redress are not effectively implemented, participants may be unable to review or correct information collected about them.
risks.evidence_quote: Generally applicable: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
risks.rationale: Without effective access and redress, individuals may have limited ability to identify or remedy privacy harms.

mitigations.description: Limit field collection to information necessary for the stated research purpose and apply the CFPB's standard privacy protections and security controls.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Using standard privacy and security controls helps reduce unnecessary collection and protects the information that is collected.

mitigations.description: Require appropriate legal agreements that establish roles, responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms before any third-party collaboration.
mitigations.evidence_quote: whether appropriate legal agreements establish roles, responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms.
mitigations.rationale: Formal agreements can constrain external use and disclosure and clarify privacy obligations.

mitigations.description: Use the CFPB's standard privacy protections and security controls for all direct, contracted, and collaborative research arrangements.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Applying the same controls across all operating models reduces the risk of inconsistent privacy handling.

mitigations.description: Limit retention and use of longitudinal field data to what is necessary for the research objective, and apply privacy protections throughout the study period.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing how long behavior-linked data is kept and used lowers the chance of prolonged tracking or secondary privacy harms.

mitigations.description: Provide specific notice and obtain meaningful consent tailored to the particular field study rather than relying only on general opportunities.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Generally applicable: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
mitigations.rationale: More tailored notice and consent improve participant understanding and control over their information.

mitigations.description: Ensure participants have effective access to their information and a workable redress process for correcting or challenging it.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Generally applicable: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
mitigations.rationale: Access and redress reduce harm by letting individuals review and address information collected about them.

risks.description: The system collects detailed mortgage application and loan data that can reveal sensitive financial and housing information about individual borrowers and applicants.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB will collect HMDA data, from certain financial institutions, that are required by Regulation C regarding originations of, purchases of, and applications for covered loans.
risks.rationale: Mortgage application and loan records can expose personal financial circumstances and housing activity.

risks.description: The data are shared with multiple federal agencies, increasing the number of entities that can access or use the information.
risks.evidence_quote: Appropriate federal agencies are member agencies of the Federal Financial Institutions Examinations Council—the Bu reau, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Board of Gov ernors of the Federal Reserve System, and the National Credit Union Administration —as well as the Department of Housing and Urban Development (collectively, “Federal HMDA agencies”).
risks.rationale: Each additional recipient expands the attack surface and the risk of inappropriate access or secondary use.

risks.description: The platform requires electronic submission of loan/application registers, which creates a risk of interception, unauthorized access, or transmission error during transfer.
risks.evidence_quote: a financial institution shall submit its loan/application register in electronic format to the appropriate federal agency at the address identified by such agency
risks.rationale: Electronic transfer of sensitive records can be exposed if transmission or submission controls fail.

risks.description: The system may enable public disclosure of mortgage lending data, which can expose individuals or small groups to re-identification or profiling if records are granular enough.
risks.evidence_quote: to assist in identifying possible discriminatory lending patterns and enforcing antidiscrimination statutes.
risks.rationale: Data used to identify lending patterns can still reveal information about specific borrowers or neighborhoods if disclosed too broadly.

risks.description: The system does not provide a public participation component, limiting individuals' ability to understand, correct, or challenge how their data are collected and used.
risks.evidence_quote: The HMDA Platform does not have a public participation component.
risks.rationale: Lack of participation reduces transparency and limits user control over personal information.

mitigations.description: Apply data minimization and collect only the HMDA fields required for the stated reporting purpose.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Provide a platform for financial institutions to report HMDA data to the Bureau.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting collection reduces the amount of sensitive borrower information held by the system.

mitigations.description: Restrict access to HMDA data to authorized personnel and agencies with a documented need to know, and log all access and sharing.
mitigations.evidence_quote: all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Tight access controls and audit logging reduce the risk created by multiple recipients.

mitigations.description: Use secure transmission methods and file validation controls for electronic submissions.
mitigations.evidence_quote: financial institutions shall submit its loan/application register in electronic format
mitigations.rationale: Secure transfer and validation help prevent interception and corrupted or unauthorized submissions.

mitigations.description: Limit public disclosure to the minimum necessary and suppress or aggregate fields that could enable re-identification.
mitigations.evidence_quote: to assist in identifying possible discriminatory lending patterns and enforcing antidiscrimination statutes.
mitigations.rationale: Aggregation and suppression preserve analytic value while reducing the chance of identifying individuals.

mitigations.description: Provide a clear public notice explaining what HMDA data are collected, how they are used, and what controls protect them.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The HMDA Platform does not have a public participation component.
mitigations.rationale: If direct participation is unavailable, clear notice is the main way to improve transparency.

risks.description: Public disclosure of HMDA data can expose borrowers' mortgage and demographic information to broader audiences than the original lenders, increasing the chance that individuals can be identified or profiled from the released records.
