risks.description: DRMS supports search and retrieval of records for audit, legal discovery, litigation holds, and FOIA inquiries, which can lead to secondary use of personal information beyond the original business purpose.
risks.evidence_quote: Specialized roles for records managers and legal staff allow for lifecycle management of records or unconstrained searching for audit, legal discover, litigation holds, or Freedom Of Information Act inquiries.
risks.rationale: Using records for multiple downstream purposes increases the chance that PII will be reused in ways data subjects did not expect.

mitigations.description: Continue encrypting the documents and databases that contain PII, and ensure the encryption is applied consistently across the stored PDF files and metadata stores.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Potential PII found in the encrypted documents includes: Name, Legal Name, Address, Tax ID number (individual or business), SSN, Data Universal Numbering System (DUNS) number, Registration in Central Contractor Registration database, Legal description of farm location, Tract Number, Deeds, Farm Shareholder salaries, Location, Farm ownership detail, Bank routing numbers, Deposit Account numbers, Contract numbers, Vendor ID.
mitigations.rationale: Encryption reduces the impact of unauthorized access to highly sensitive records.

mitigations.description: Enforce the stated role-based access restrictions so staff can only upload and search documents within their organizational role and rights.
mitigations.evidence_quote: All staff are able to upload and search for documents, limited by their organizational role and rights.
mitigations.rationale: Tight role enforcement limits unnecessary exposure of personal information.

mitigations.description: Limit unconstrained searching to only those cases where it is required and document approvals for records-manager and legal-staff searches.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting broad search capability lowers the risk of over-disclosure during legal and records-management activities.

mitigations.description: Validate uploads from customers and auditors before ingestion to reduce the chance that incorrect or unnecessary PII is entered into TeamMate+.
mitigations.rationale: Pre-ingestion review helps prevent inaccurate or excessive personal data from being stored.

mitigations.description: Apply the least-privilege model and need-to-know approvals to contractor access, with periodic review of contractor accounts and permissions.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Department contractors with a need-to-know will have access to Pipeline FPAC Mod as part of their regular assigned duties.
mitigations.rationale: Periodic permission review helps ensure contractors retain only the access required for their duties.

mitigations.description: Review retention schedules to minimize unnecessary retention and ensure records are destroyed or archived according to the approved NARA schedule.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Information on most applications is retained indefinitely (permanent records).
mitigations.rationale: Reducing retention to what is required shortens the time that PII remains exposed to risk.

mitigations.description: Restrict FOIA, litigation-hold, audit, and legal-discovery access to the minimum records needed for each request or case.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Specialized roles for records managers and legal staff allow for lifecycle management of records or unconstrained searching for audit, legal discover, litigation holds, or Freedom Of Information Act inquiries.
mitigations.rationale: Need-to-know limits help prevent secondary use of records beyond the specific purpose.

risks.description: The system stores highly sensitive identifiers, including SSNs and EINs, which creates a risk of identity theft or other harm if the data is exposed.
risks.evidence_quote: Name, Address, Phone Numbers, SSN, EIN number, eAuth JD/Name, Farm IDs
risks.rationale: SSNs and EINs are highly sensitive direct identifiers, so exposure would create significant privacy harm.

risks.description: Information is retained indefinitely for most applications, increasing the chance that unnecessary records remain available long after they are needed.
risks.evidence_quote: Information on most applications is retained indefinitely (permanent records).
risks.rationale: Long retention expands the window in which records can be accessed, disclosed, or misused.

risks.description: The system shares policy information with external Approved Insurance Providers, creating a risk of unauthorized or overbroad disclosure outside USDA.
risks.evidence_quote: Policy information is shared only with the Approved insurance Providers (AIP).
risks.rationale: External sharing increases the number of parties that can access the data and therefore the disclosure risk.

risks.description: The system shares data with an internal fraud-analysis division, which could lead to secondary use of personal data beyond the original collection purpose if access is not tightly limited.
risks.evidence_quote: This group performs the forensic data mining of RMA's data, looking for indications of Fraud, Waste, and Abuse.
risks.rationale: Fraud-mining uses can expose sensitive records to broader internal review and secondary analysis.

risks.description: Contractors have access to the system, creating a risk that non-federal personnel may view or handle PII without sufficient need-to-know controls.
risks.evidence_quote: Will Department contractors have access to the system? Yes
risks.rationale: Contractor access expands the population with potential access to PII.

risks.description: The system hosts many applications on a shared platform, which can increase the risk of cross-application exposure or broader-than-necessary access to PII.
risks.evidence_quote: The Pipeline RMA HVA serves as the security boundary for all former operational RMA HVA applications with a “Low” or “Moderate” FIPS assessment result.
risks.rationale: A shared boundary for many applications can make access control and isolation harder to maintain.

risks.description: The system receives data from insurance agents and loss adjusters through AIPs, which creates a risk that inaccurate or outdated personal data will be stored and used for eligibility or payment decisions.
risks.evidence_quote: Approved Insurance Providers (AIP) provide data to RMA that is collected from Insurance Agents and Loss Adjusters
risks.rationale: Data passed through multiple parties can be stale or incorrect when it reaches the system.

risks.description: The system uses third-party websites to generate escrow payment amounts, which creates a risk of indirect disclosure or processing beyond what is necessary even if the third party is not supposed to handle PII.
risks.evidence_quote: The use of Third Party websites is restricted to generating the Escrow payment amount for an AIP. No PII or financial information is processed by the third party application.
risks.rationale: Any third-party integration creates some risk of data leakage or unintended processing, even when limited.

mitigations.description: Limit access to SSNs and EINs to only the specific roles and applications that require them, and encrypt them both in transit and at rest.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The AIP's use the Pipeline RMA HVA system to collect and provide to FCIC all SSNs or EINs that are required to be submitted by the policyholder under the eligible crop insurance contract
mitigations.rationale: Restricting and protecting direct identifiers reduces the likelihood and impact of exposure.

mitigations.description: Apply record-specific retention limits and periodic disposition reviews so records are not kept longer than required by the approved schedule.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The archiving and retention strategy for applications on Pipeline RMA HVA will be retained in accordance with the NARA Retention Schedule.
mitigations.rationale: Following a defined retention schedule reduces unnecessary accumulation of personal data.

mitigations.description: Use written data-sharing agreements and role-based access controls for AIPs, and limit shared fields to only what is needed for policy verification.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Policy information is shared only with the Approved insurance Providers (AIP). These are the very entities that collect the information.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing the fields shared externally lowers the risk of over-disclosure.

mitigations.description: Constrain fraud-mining access to approved analysts, log queries and exports, and review use of the data for purpose limitation.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The data is primarily shared with the RMA Strategic Data Analysis Division.
mitigations.rationale: Tight controls and auditing help ensure secondary use stays within authorized purposes.

mitigations.description: Require contractor access to be granted only on a need-to-know basis with training, least-privilege permissions, and monitoring.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Will Department contractors have access to the system? Yes
mitigations.rationale: Least-privilege access reduces the chance that contractors see more PII than necessary.

mitigations.description: Maintain strict segmentation and separate access controls among the hosted applications to prevent cross-application exposure.
mitigations.evidence_quote: This system hosts several RMA High Value Asset (HVA) applications.
mitigations.rationale: Segmentation helps ensure one application's users or data do not spill into another.

mitigations.description: Validate and reconcile incoming data with source records before using it for eligibility or payment decisions.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The information is collected via hard copy forms and e-forms completed by the insured producer, insurance agent, or adjustor.
mitigations.rationale: Validation reduces the chance that incorrect data affects individuals' benefits or eligibility.

mitigations.description: Limit the third-party website to the minimum necessary function, prohibit PII transfer, and periodically review the integration for compliance.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The use of Third Party websites is restricted to generating the Escrow payment amount for an AIP. No PII or financial information is processed by the third party application.
mitigations.rationale: Keeping the third-party use narrow reduces the chance of unintended disclosure.

risks.description: The CFPB may collect personally identifiable information from people who interact with it on social media, creating a privacy risk if that data is exposed or misused.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may collect or use a limited amount of Personally Identifiable Information (“PII”) when using social media to further its ability to interact with the public.
risks.rationale: Any collection of PII creates risk because it can identify individuals and is sensitive if handled improperly.

risks.description: Social media interactions occur on third-party platforms, so user information may be subject to the platform operators' practices and controls rather than only CFPB's.
risks.evidence_quote: Social media platforms are generally controlled and operated by non-government third parties.
risks.rationale: Third-party control can reduce the agency's ability to fully govern how personal information is processed.

risks.description: Users may not understand what privacy protections apply when they interact with CFPB through social media, increasing the risk of unexpected disclosure or sharing.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB understands that the public expects certain privacy protections when interacting with the Bureau through social media.
risks.rationale: When privacy expectations are unclear, people may share information they would not otherwise disclose.

risks.description: The system may collect identifiers such as IP address, geographic information, or demographic information, which can enable tracking or profiling of individuals.
risks.evidence_quote: PII is any information that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual’s identity such as name, username, email address, Internet Protocol (IP) address, geographic information, or demographic information.
risks.rationale: These data elements can reveal identity or location and increase the sensitivity of the interaction.

risks.description: Information collected through social media could be retained or reused under the related system of records, which may expand the privacy impact beyond the original interaction.
risks.evidence_quote: To the extent that the CFPB may collect PII through social media interactions, this information would be covered by the Social Networks and Citizen Engagement System (CFPB.006) System of Records Notice.
risks.rationale: Coverage under a system of records means the information may be stored and managed in a way that extends its privacy footprint.

mitigations.description: Limit collection of PII on social media to the minimum needed for the interaction and avoid collecting unnecessary identifiers.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB may collect or use a limited amount of Personally Identifiable Information (“PII”) when using social media to further its ability to interact with the public.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing PII reduces the amount of sensitive data that could be exposed or misused.

mitigations.description: Apply CFPB privacy and security requirements to social media activities and account for the limits of third-party platform control.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Agency controls can reduce risk even when the underlying platform is operated by a third party.

mitigations.description: Provide clear notice to users about how privacy works on CFPB social media channels and what protections apply before they share information.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB understands that the public expects certain privacy protections when interacting with the Bureau through social media.
mitigations.rationale: Clear notice helps align user behavior with actual privacy conditions and reduces surprise disclosures.

mitigations.description: Restrict collection and handling of sensitive identifiers such as IP address, geographic information, and demographic information to what is necessary for the stated purpose.
mitigations.evidence_quote: PII is any information that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual’s identity such as name, username, email address, Internet Protocol (IP) address, geographic information, or demographic information.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting use of these identifiers lowers the chance of tracking or unintended inference about individuals.

mitigations.description: Apply the Social Networks and Citizen Engagement System (CFPB.006) records controls consistently to any PII collected through social media.
mitigations.evidence_quote: To the extent that the CFPB may collect PII through social media interactions, this information would be covered by the Social Networks and Citizen Engagement System (CFPB.006) System of Records Notice.
mitigations.rationale: Using the applicable system-of-records controls helps ensure collected information is governed and protected.

risks.description: The system republishes publicly available counselor data and makes it easier to search and download, which can increase exposure of agency contact details and other associated information beyond the original source.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB is increasing access to the HUD counselor dataset in an effort to make the information more useful to the public
risks.rationale: Making the dataset easier to access and reuse increases the chance that information about individuals associated with agencies will be broadly disseminated.

risks.description: Users can download or share the dataset in multiple formats, which creates a risk of further redistribution and reuse outside CFPB control.
risks.evidence_quote: The HUD API and the CFPB housing counselor locator tool also enables users to download or share data in the HUD counselor dataset in a variety of formats.
risks.rationale: Downloadable and shareable outputs are harder to contain once released to the public.

risks.description: The API can be used by third-party developers and lenders to build their own applications or systems, which may lead to repurposing of the data in ways that increase privacy exposure.
risks.evidence_quote: The API, owned and managed by HUD, enables users to retrieve the HUD counselor dataset and use that data for their own applications or systems outside of CFPB.
risks.rationale: Third-party reuse expands the number of environments where the data may be stored, combined, or disclosed.

risks.description: The locator tool collects ZIP codes from users, which can reveal location information and potentially be linked to an individual's search behavior.
risks.evidence_quote: PII collected from users of the CFPB housing counselor locator tool includes:  ZIP code entered for search results.
risks.rationale: ZIP codes are location data and can be sensitive when tied to repeated or contextualized searches.

risks.description: The system retains ZIP codes and user analytics as permanent records until a disposition schedule is approved, increasing the duration of exposure for user activity data.
risks.evidence_quote: records collected through consumerfinance.gov (user analytics and ZIP codes entered in the locator tool) are being managed as permanent records until the disposition schedule for these records is approved by the National Archives and Records Administration
risks.rationale: Long retention increases the window during which collected user data can be accessed or misused.

risks.description: The system collects non-identifying analytics such as visit timestamps, browser version, pages viewed, and time on site, which can be used to profile or infer user behavior when combined with other data.
risks.evidence_quote: consumerfinance.gov collects other non‐identifying information from users of the CFPB housing counselor locator tool as part of normal operations supporting website functionality and security, (e.g. visit timestamps, browser version and operating system, pages viewed and time on site, etc.)
risks.rationale: Even non-identifying telemetry can become privacy-relevant when analyzed over time or combined with other records.

risks.description: There is no authorization process for read-only access, so anyone can access the dataset and locator tool without restriction, increasing the risk of mass collection and secondary use.
risks.evidence_quote: There is no authorization process for read-only access to the dataset or for use of the CFPB housing counselor locator tool.
risks.rationale: Open access makes it easier for anyone to harvest or aggregate the information at scale.

mitigations.description: Limit the public-facing dataset to the minimum fields needed for locating counseling agencies and avoid exposing unnecessary personal contact details where possible.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing the amount of exposed data lowers the privacy impact of public republication.

mitigations.description: Add usage terms or technical controls that discourage bulk downloading and unauthorized redistribution of the dataset.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting bulk reuse helps reduce uncontrolled downstream dissemination.

mitigations.description: Provide clear reuse guidance and API terms that restrict downstream use to purposes consistent with the housing counseling program and applicable rules.
mitigations.rationale: Clear conditions on reuse can reduce privacy risks from third-party applications built on the data.

mitigations.description: Minimize collection of ZIP codes by using them only to produce search results and avoid retaining them longer than necessary for that purpose.
mitigations.evidence_quote: ZIP codes entered by users of the locator tool are collected in order to provide users with a list of HUD‐approved housing counseling agencies within a specified range of their input ZIP code.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting collection and retention of location data reduces the privacy impact of user searches.

mitigations.description: Finalize and implement a NARA-approved disposition schedule for consumerfinance.gov analytics and ZIP code records as soon as possible.
mitigations.evidence_quote: records collected through consumerfinance.gov (user analytics and ZIP codes entered in the locator tool) are being managed as permanent records until the disposition schedule for these records is approved by the National Archives and Records Administration
mitigations.rationale: Approved retention limits reduce the period during which user data remains exposed.

mitigations.description: Limit analytics collection to what is necessary for website functionality, security, and usability evaluation, and avoid retaining detailed browsing telemetry longer than needed.
mitigations.evidence_quote: consumerfinance.gov collects other non‐identifying information from users of the CFPB housing counselor locator tool as part of normal operations supporting website functionality and security, (e.g. visit timestamps, browser version and operating system, pages viewed and time on site, etc.) for consumerfinance.gov, and to evaluate usability of the tool.
mitigations.rationale: Collecting only necessary telemetry and limiting retention reduces the chance of behavioral profiling.

mitigations.description: Add rate limiting or anti-scraping controls to the public tool and API to reduce mass harvesting of the dataset.
mitigations.rationale: Technical access controls can reduce the risk created by unrestricted public read-only access.

risks.description: The system can include direct identifiers and sensitive data, so a breach or misuse could expose names, contact details, SSNs, financial account numbers, biometric information, or health information.
risks.evidence_quote: In certain circumstances, Administrative Data collected for Market Research may include direct identifying PII, including: • Name • Phone number • Home address • Email • Financial account number
risks.rationale: The presence of direct identifiers and sensitive categories increases the harm if the data is improperly accessed or disclosed.

risks.description: Matching records across datasets can create new combined profiles and increase the chance of re-identification even when direct identifiers are removed.
risks.evidence_quote: Market Research may involve the matching of records across different datasets.
risks.rationale: Linking datasets can make individuals more identifiable than any single dataset alone.

risks.description: Using unique record locators and updates from external entities can enable ongoing linkage of records over time, which may expand profiling risk.
risks.evidence_quote: the CFPB may obtain updates or supplements to a dataset and, in those circumstances, may use record locators unique to the entity providing the update in order to update or supplement the individual records.
risks.rationale: Persistent linkage mechanisms can make it easier to track the same person across datasets and time.

risks.description: The system may use demographic information such as race, gender, age, education, and income, which can create sensitivity and fairness concerns if combined with financial data.
risks.evidence_quote: Demographic information, such as race/ethnicity, gender, age, education level, and income
risks.rationale: Combining demographic traits with financial records can reveal sensitive patterns about people or groups.

risks.description: The CFPB relies on third parties and public databases for notice, so affected individuals may not receive direct notice from the CFPB about collection or sharing of their data.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB collects Administrative Data only from third parties, commercial sources and public databases, not directly from consumers, and it is those third parties’ responsibility to determine whether notice is required and to provide any requisite notice.
risks.rationale: When notice depends on outside parties, individuals may be unaware their information is being used for research.

risks.description: Indefinite retention of computer and paper records increases the amount of time personal information remains available for unauthorized access, secondary use, or future disclosure.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Longer retention generally increases exposure because the data remains available for a longer period.

risks.description: Sharing results with the general public, data sources, and federal financial regulators could still create disclosure risk if outputs are not sufficiently aggregated or if small-cell data is released.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share the results of Market Research with the general public, the source of the Administrative Data, and/or federal financial regulators.
risks.rationale: Broader dissemination raises the chance that released results could be linked back to individuals.

risks.description: Because the CFPB may use data from commercial sources and public databases, there is a risk that collected information is inaccurate, outdated, or mismatched, leading to incorrect inferences about people or markets.
risks.evidence_quote: Administrative Data is gathered from third parties, such as those that offer or provide consumer financial products or services, from commercial sources, and from public databases.
risks.rationale: Third-party and public-source data can contain errors that affect the quality and fairness of analysis.

mitigations.description: Limit collection and storage of direct identifiers and sensitive fields to only what is necessary, and separate them from analytic datasets whenever possible.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB collects Administrative Data to carry out its statutory mandates with emphasis on promoting efficiency and minimizing burdens posed by the collection.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing the amount of identifying and sensitive data lowers the impact of any unauthorized access.

mitigations.description: Apply de-identification after record matching and restrict access to the matched dataset until identifiers are removed.
mitigations.evidence_quote: After the matching is complete, a de-identified copy of the matched dataset will be used for conducting research and analysis.
mitigations.rationale: De-identifying the matched dataset reduces the chance that linked records can be tied back to individuals.

mitigations.description: Minimize use of persistent record locators and delete or tokenize them once updates and matching are complete.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting durable linkage keys reduces the ability to track the same person across datasets over time.

mitigations.description: Use only the demographic attributes needed for the specific research question and suppress or aggregate sensitive subgroup outputs before release.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting and aggregating demographic data reduces the chance of sensitive or unfairly targeted conclusions.

mitigations.description: Provide CFPB-issued notice or public transparency about the categories of third-party, commercial, and public-source data used in Market Research.
mitigations.rationale: Direct transparency helps affected people understand how their information may be used even when collection is indirect.

mitigations.description: Adopt and follow a fixed records disposition schedule approved by NARA as soon as possible, and purge records when the schedule permits.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Records that fall under a general records schedule will be disposed of according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.rationale: A defined retention limit reduces how long data remains exposed to misuse or breach.

mitigations.description: Review all public and external releases for re-identification risk and suppress small cells or other identifying details before sharing.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Any such results do not include information that directly identifies any individual.
mitigations.rationale: Pre-release review helps ensure shared results stay aggregated and non-identifying.

mitigations.description: Validate, reconcile, and document data quality issues when using third-party, commercial, and public-source data.
mitigations.rationale: Data quality checks reduce the risk of inaccurate or misleading profiles and analyses.

risks.description: Even though the dataset removes direct identifiers, users may still isolate a single loan record and infer information about a person or household from the remaining loan and property details.
risks.evidence_quote: Users may be able to isolate a single record, but the record will not contain any direct identifiers.
risks.rationale: A record that can be singled out can still create privacy exposure through inference when combined with the detailed fields in the dataset.

risks.description: The dataset includes sensitive mortgage and property details that could reveal financial circumstances and location-related information about applicants and borrowers.
risks.evidence_quote: The HMDA Public Use Dataset includes the following information: • Loan data o Application year o Loan or application type, purpose, amount (rounded to nearest thousand) o Action taken and denial reason, if applicable o Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act (HOEPA) flag o Lien status (first, subordinate, unsecured) o Rate spread on higher-priced mortgages o Purchaser type o Preapproval request • Property data o Census tract, Metropolitan Statistical Area or Metropolitan Division, State, County o Property type
risks.rationale: Detailed loan and geography fields can reveal personal financial status and where a person lives or sought credit.

risks.description: The dataset is publicly available to anyone, including agencies and private sector organizations, so there is broad risk of secondary use, mass analysis, or re-identification attempts.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB is republishing, on consumerfinance.gov, a Dataset that is publicly available on the FFIEC website. As with the dataset available on the FFIEC website, the HMDA Public Use Dataset will be available to the public, including federal and state agencies and private sector organizations.
risks.rationale: Open public access increases the number of potential users and the likelihood that the data will be combined with other sources.

risks.description: The API allows users to query, filter, visualize, download, and share the data in multiple formats, which increases the chance that someone can reconstruct or spotlight a particular record.
risks.evidence_quote: The data publishing API permits users to create visualizations from the Dataset and to query and filter the Dataset to create custom summary tables. The data publishing API also enables users to download or share data in the Dataset in a variety of formats.
risks.rationale: Flexible access and export tools make it easier to isolate records and redistribute them widely.

risks.description: CFPB republishes the dataset without independently verifying accuracy or completeness, so any errors in the source data may be propagated to the public and harm individuals through incorrect inferences.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB accepts the HMDA Public Use Dataset from the FFIEC as accurate and complete, and does not alter the data or independently verify the accuracy and completeness of the dataset before republishing it on consumerfinance.gov.
risks.rationale: If inaccurate data is republished, individuals may be affected by mistaken conclusions drawn from the dataset.

risks.description: The system retains the dataset until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA, which may extend the period that sensitive mortgage data remains available for privacy exposure.
risks.evidence_quote: The HMDA Public Use Dataset is currently retained in accordance with the Federal Reserve Board Schedule N1-082-05-1, Home Mortgage Disclosure Act and Related Records. The CFPB will continue to retain these records until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA.
risks.rationale: Longer retention increases the window during which public data can be reused, linked, or analyzed.

risks.description: Although the public is told that mortgage applicants are asked about ethnicity, race, and sex, the system still republishes data derived from those disclosures, creating risk of sensitive attribute exposure through public analysis.
risks.evidence_quote: Lenders are required to inform mortgage applicants that the Federal government requests information concerning the ethnicity, race, and sex of the applicant in order to monitor compliance with Federal statutes that prohibit lenders from discriminating against applicants on these bases.
risks.rationale: Public release of data tied to protected characteristics can enable sensitive profiling even when direct identifiers are removed.

risks.description: Operations staff have access to the non-public database layer, so there is a risk of unauthorized internal access or misuse if access controls are not properly enforced.
risks.evidence_quote: CFPB Operations staff has access to the database layer for maintenance purposes. Access to this layer is granted through the CFPB Access Control Process and in accordance with the CFPB Acceptable Use Policy.
risks.rationale: Any internal maintenance access creates a need to prevent inappropriate access or disclosure.

mitigations.description: Continue to suppress direct identifiers and apply additional statistical disclosure controls to reduce the chance that a single record can be singled out.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The HMDA Public Use Dataset does not include any information that directly identifies an individual.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing identifiability lowers the risk that a user can infer a person's loan or property details from one record.

mitigations.description: Keep limiting the dataset to the public-use fields needed for disclosure and maintain rounding or other masking of sensitive numeric values.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Loan data o Application year o Loan or application type, purpose, amount (rounded to nearest thousand)
mitigations.rationale: Limiting detail and masking values reduces the amount of personal financial information exposed.

mitigations.description: Publish prominent guidance warning users not to attempt re-identification or linkage with other datasets and to use the data only for lawful purposes.
mitigations.rationale: Clear use restrictions can reduce misuse when data is broadly available to the public.

mitigations.description: Add rate limits, download safeguards, and query monitoring to the API to make bulk extraction and record isolation harder.
mitigations.rationale: Technical controls can reduce the ability to rapidly query, extract, or reconstruct sensitive records.

mitigations.description: Implement validation checks and periodic quality review before republication to catch obvious source-data errors.
mitigations.evidence_quote: CFPB does use automated controls to ensure integrity of the HMDA Public Use Dataset received from the FFIEC and republished on consumerfinance.gov.
mitigations.rationale: Basic validation helps prevent inaccurate data from being republished and misused.

mitigations.description: Adopt and publish a CFPB-specific retention schedule as soon as possible and delete or archive data according to that approved schedule.
mitigations.rationale: A defined retention schedule limits unnecessary long-term exposure of public mortgage data.

mitigations.description: Provide contextual notices explaining that the dataset is public-use and that it may be used to monitor lending patterns involving protected classes.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Both HMDA and Regulation C provide notice to the public that federal agencies, including the CFPB, will collect the data that comprises the HMDA Public Use Dataset.
mitigations.rationale: Contextual notice helps users understand the sensitivity of the data and the privacy implications of analysis.

mitigations.description: Limit database-layer access to the minimum number of staff needed and review access periodically under the existing access-control process.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Access to this layer is granted through the CFPB Access Control Process and in accordance with the CFPB Acceptable Use Policy.
mitigations.rationale: Least-privilege access and periodic review reduce the chance of internal misuse or accidental disclosure.

risks.description: The system collects highly sensitive direct identifiers, including Social Security numbers, which creates a risk of identity theft or unauthorized re-identification if exposed.
risks.evidence_quote: Consumer Experience Research typically uses the following direct identifying PII to facilitate and administer Consumer Experience Research:  Names  Phone number  Email address  Mailing address  Social Security number
risks.rationale: SSNs and other direct identifiers are especially sensitive because they can directly identify respondents and enable misuse if disclosed.

risks.description: The system collects sensitive personal and potentially stigmatizing information such as health conditions, foreclosure, debt collections, and public benefits status, which could cause harm if disclosed or used improperly.
risks.evidence_quote: Response Data may also contain demographic information, such as race/ethnicity, gender, age, education level, income; and other sensitive information, such as a consumer’s experience with foreclosure or debt collections; existing health condition that impacts access to types of products/services; or status of enrollment in public benefits.
risks.rationale: Sensitive attributes increase the privacy impact of any disclosure because they reveal intimate financial, health, and socioeconomic details.

risks.description: Matching response data with administrative data such as credit score and balances can create new assembled profiles that increase re-identification and inference risk.
risks.evidence_quote: In some cases, Consumer Experience Research may involve the matching of records, such as credit score to Response Data, creating new assemblies of information about the Respondent.
risks.rationale: Combining datasets can reveal more about a person than any single source and can make individuals easier to identify.

risks.description: The system uses administrative data and contact information to identify potential survey recipients, which can expose people to outreach based on third-party data they may not expect.
risks.evidence_quote: CFPB may also match Administrative Data to contact information in order to identify potential recipients of surveys and then use those surveys to solicit information on consumer experiences with consumer financial products and services.
risks.rationale: Using third-party records for targeting can create privacy expectations issues and may reveal participation in a research program.

risks.description: The system may collect additional information from third parties with consent, creating a risk that respondents do not fully understand what external data will be obtained or how it will be used.
risks.evidence_quote: Consumer Experience Research primarily relies on information collected directly from the individual and subject to the individual’s consent for the CFPB to collect additional information from third parties, such as those that offer or provide consumer financial products or services.
risks.rationale: Third-party collection expands the scope of data processing and can undermine informed consent if not clearly explained.

risks.description: The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until a NARA schedule is approved, which increases the chance of long-term exposure or secondary use beyond the original purpose.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Long retention increases the window in which data can be breached, misused, or repurposed.

risks.description: Research outputs may be shared externally, including to the general public, which creates a risk of residual disclosure even after aggregation and disclosure-protection procedures.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share products of Consumer Experience Research externally, including by disseminating research results to the general public.
risks.rationale: Public dissemination broadens access and can still leak information if de-identification controls are imperfect.

risks.description: The system may disclose direct identifying PII in external products such as case studies or quotes, which could expose respondents unless consent is properly managed.
risks.evidence_quote: In some cases where the CPFB seeks to share direct identifying PII in an external product, e.g. case study or quote, the CFBP will obtain consent of the appropriate Respondents prior to disclosure.
risks.rationale: Publishing identifiable examples can directly reveal a respondent’s participation or personal information.

risks.description: Data transfers between contractor systems, vendor websites, and CFPB internal systems rely on encrypted tunnels and encrypted email, but any transmission process still presents a risk of interception or misdelivery.
risks.evidence_quote: Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated data transfers between contractor systems and/or vendor websites and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels. These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
risks.rationale: Even encrypted transfers can be vulnerable to operational errors or endpoint compromise during transmission.

mitigations.description: Minimize collection of SSNs and other direct identifiers to only cases where they are strictly necessary, and keep them stored separately from research data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: When direct identifying PII is necessary to facilitate Consumer Experience Research rather than necessary to the analysis, the direct identifying PII is stored and secured separately.
mitigations.rationale: Separating and minimizing direct identifiers reduces the chance that sensitive identity data will be exposed with research content.

mitigations.description: Apply strict access controls and disclosure-protection procedures to sensitive response data before any sharing or publication.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB does not typically share the Response Data generated in the course of Consumer Experience Research in un-aggregated form, unless it is stripped of direct identifying PII and subject to disclosure-protection procedures.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting exposure of sensitive attributes lowers the risk of harmful disclosure.

mitigations.description: Use de-identified copies of matched datasets for analysis and remove direct identifiers immediately after matching is complete.
mitigations.evidence_quote: After the matching is complete, a de- identified copy of the matched dataset is used for conducting research and analysis.
mitigations.rationale: De-identifying matched data reduces the risk that combined records can be tied back to specific people.

mitigations.description: Limit use of administrative data for survey targeting to the minimum necessary and document the purpose and scope of each matching activity.
mitigations.evidence_quote: CFPB may also match Administrative Data to contact information in order to identify potential recipients of surveys and then use those surveys to solicit information on consumer experiences with consumer financial products and services.
mitigations.rationale: Narrowing the use of third-party data reduces unnecessary exposure of people’s contact and participation information.

mitigations.description: Provide clear, specific consent notices that explain what third-party data will be collected, from whom, and for what purpose.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Consumer Experience Research primarily relies on information collected directly from the individual and subject to the individual’s consent for the CFPB to collect additional information from third parties, such as those that offer or provide consumer financial products or services.
mitigations.rationale: Specific consent improves transparency and helps respondents understand external data collection.

mitigations.description: Implement and enforce a records disposition schedule as soon as possible so data are not held indefinitely without a retention limit.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
mitigations.rationale: A defined retention period reduces the amount of data exposed over time.

mitigations.description: Continue applying aggregation, rounding, variable suppression, and observation exclusion before releasing research products externally.
mitigations.evidence_quote: These external products are subject to disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation of response categories, rounding, exclusion of some variables, or exclusion of observations, and typically do not include direct identifying PII.
mitigations.rationale: These techniques reduce the likelihood that public reports reveal individual respondents.

mitigations.description: Require documented respondent consent before including any direct identifying PII in case studies, quotes, or other external products.
mitigations.evidence_quote: If the CPFB seeks to share direct identifying PII in an external product, it will obtain consent of the appropriate Respondents prior to disclosure.
mitigations.rationale: Consent is a direct safeguard for any publication that could identify a person.

mitigations.description: Maintain encryption for all transfers and add transfer controls such as validation, logging, and recipient verification for non-automated exchanges.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated data transfers between contractor systems and/or vendor websites and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels. These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
mitigations.rationale: Additional transfer controls help reduce the risk of accidental or unauthorized disclosure during manual exchanges.

risks.description: The system may include highly sensitive direct identifiers such as SSNs, financial account numbers, home addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or re-identification.
risks.evidence_quote: In some cases, they may include direct identifying PII, including: • Name • Phone number • Home address • Email • Financial account number • Social Security number
risks.rationale: These identifiers can directly expose individuals if accessed or shared improperly.

risks.description: The system may include biometric information and health or medical information, which increases the sensitivity and potential harm of any disclosure.
risks.evidence_quote: Other Information (including biometric information and health or medical information)
risks.rationale: Sensitive data types can cause greater privacy harm than ordinary contact or demographic information.

risks.description: Individuals generally do not receive notice when their information is collected or used, limiting transparency and informed awareness.
risks.evidence_quote: individuals generally will not receive notice that the information is being requested and therefore how such information will be used or disclosed.
risks.rationale: Lack of notice makes it harder for people to understand or challenge how their data is handled.

risks.description: Individuals generally do not receive notice when their information is shared, which can obscure downstream disclosures and uses.
risks.evidence_quote: individuals generally will not be informed of PII collected through supervisory or enforcement activity, or receive notice as to how information will be used or disclosed.
risks.rationale: Without disclosure notice, affected people cannot know where their information goes.

risks.description: The CFPB may match records across datasets and update or supplement records, which can create new linked profiles or reveal additional information about individuals.
risks.evidence_quote: Use of SEFL Data for Market Research may involve the matching of records across different datasets.
risks.rationale: Linking datasets can increase the amount and sensitivity of information associated with a person.

risks.description: The CFPB may use direct identifying PII to contact potential survey recipients, creating a risk of unwanted outreach or exposure of participation in a supervisory or enforcement-related context.
risks.evidence_quote: When the CFPB does use direct identifying PII in analyses, it does so in order to a) match across datasets; b) update data sets; and c) contact potential recipients of surveys
risks.rationale: Contacting people based on regulatory data can reveal their relationship to the CFPB or to consumer finance issues.

risks.description: The system may use unique record locators and other linked data to update or supplement individual records, which can increase the risk of persistent tracking over time.
risks.evidence_quote: may use record locators unique to the entity providing the update in order to update or supplement the individual records.
risks.rationale: Persistent record linkage can make it easier to maintain long-lived profiles.

risks.description: The CFPB retains records indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, increasing the window for misuse, breach, or secondary use.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Long retention generally increases exposure time and the consequences of any future access event.

risks.description: The system may share products of market research with the general public and federal financial regulators, which could create disclosure risk if aggregation or de-identification fails.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share the products of Market Research with the general public and federal financial regulators.
risks.rationale: Public release widens access and raises the stakes for any residual identifiability.

mitigations.description: Minimize collection and use of direct identifiers, and keep them separated from research datasets whenever possible.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Typically, direct identifying PII has been stripped from SEFL Data used for Market Research.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing direct identifiers lowers the chance of unauthorized identification.

mitigations.description: Apply stricter access controls and handling rules for biometric and health or medical information, with use limited to cases where it is strictly necessary.
mitigations.rationale: Extra safeguards are warranted because the system explicitly includes highly sensitive data.

mitigations.description: Provide notice whenever practicable, and use the PIA’s constructive notice in a clear, accessible form when direct notice is not possible.
mitigations.evidence_quote: In cases where notice cannot be provided or is not required, the CFPB has provided constructive notice of how it may use such information through this PIA.
mitigations.rationale: Clear notice improves transparency even when direct notice is unavailable.

mitigations.description: Limit disclosures to the smallest necessary set of recipients and document each disclosure under the applicable SORN and disclosure rules.
mitigations.evidence_quote: the CFPB may share information as outlined in the Routine Uses of each applicable SORN.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting disclosures to authorized routine uses reduces unnecessary sharing.

mitigations.description: Use privacy-preserving record linkage methods and retain only the de-identified matched dataset for analysis after matching is complete.
mitigations.evidence_quote: After the matching is complete, a de-identified copy of the matched dataset is used for conducting Market Research and analysis.
mitigations.rationale: Removing identifiers after linkage reduces the chance that linked profiles can be traced back to individuals.

mitigations.description: Limit survey outreach to cases where it is necessary, and avoid contacting individuals when the same research can be completed with de-identified or aggregated data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: contact potential recipients of surveys and then use those surveys to solicit information on consumer experiences with consumer financial products and services.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing outreach limits exposure of individuals to contact based on sensitive regulatory data.

mitigations.description: Restrict use of record locators to narrowly defined update tasks and discard or sever them once the update is complete.
mitigations.evidence_quote: may use record locators unique to the entity providing the update in order to update or supplement the individual records.
mitigations.rationale: Temporary use of locators reduces the risk of long-term linkage and tracking.

mitigations.description: Adopt and obtain approval of a records disposition schedule as soon as possible so records are not held indefinitely.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB will continue to retain these records until a CFPB records schedule is approved by the National Archives and Records Administration.
mitigations.rationale: A disposition schedule limits unnecessary long-term retention.

mitigations.description: Review all public-facing market research products for re-identification risk before release and suppress or aggregate any small cells or unique combinations.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share the products of Market Research with the general public and federal financial regulators. Any such results do not include information that directly identifies any individual.
mitigations.rationale: Pre-release review helps ensure public outputs remain non-identifying.

risks.description: The system may retain participant records indefinitely, increasing the chance that personal information remains exposed longer than necessary.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until the National Archives and Records Administration (“NARA”) approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Long retention expands the window during which data could be misused, breached, or repurposed beyond the original need.

risks.description: The system may collect highly sensitive information, including SSNs, financial data, biometric information, and health or medical information.
risks.evidence_quote: Name and other biographic information (e.g. date of birth) Contact Information (address, zip code, telephone number, email address) Social Security number (SSN) or other identifier Financial Information User and Online Information Third Party Information Other Information (including biometric information and health or medical information)
risks.rationale: Sensitive data creates elevated harm if improperly accessed or disclosed.

risks.description: The system may match direct identifiers with response data and administrative data to create new information about participants.
risks.evidence_quote: In some special cases, Consumer Education may involve the matching of records, such as credit score to Response Data, creating new information about the Participant.
risks.rationale: Linking datasets can reveal more about a person than any single source alone and increases privacy impact.

risks.description: The system may collect and use administrative data such as credit scores, account balances, payment histories, and remediation details, which can reveal financial behavior and status.
risks.evidence_quote: it may at times include Administrative Data regarding an individual’s habits or experiences related to specific financial products or services, such as credit scores, account balances, payment histories.
risks.rationale: Financial behavior data is sensitive because it can expose a participant’s economic circumstances and choices.

risks.description: The system may collect website and online tool usage data, including IP address and visit timestamps, which can be used to track user activity across sessions.
risks.evidence_quote: how visitors are using the website or tools (including IP address, visit timestamps, browser version and operating system, pages viewed, time on the site, the day and time of access, and the address that linked the user directly to the website or tool)
risks.rationale: Even when described as aggregate, these data points can support detailed behavioral profiling if not tightly controlled.

risks.description: The system may receive information from third parties that offer or provide consumer financial products or services, creating a risk of collecting data without participants fully understanding the scope of sharing.
risks.evidence_quote: Consumer Education primarily relies on information collected directly from the individual and with the individual’s consent to collect information from third parties, such as those that offer or provide consumer financial products or services.
risks.rationale: Third-party collection can broaden the data footprint and make consent and transparency more difficult.

risks.description: The system may share response data in un-aggregated form in some cases, which could expose participant-level information to recipients.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB does not typically share Response Data generated in the course of Consumer Education in un-aggregated form. When the CFPB does share Response Data, the CFPB provides notice to the Participants through the notice mechanisms discussed in Section 2.2, and Participants can then choose whether they want to participate given that sharing.
risks.rationale: Un-aggregated sharing increases the chance that individuals could be re-identified or profiled.

risks.description: The system allows some information to be retrieved by personal identifier, which can increase the risk of unauthorized identification or access.
risks.evidence_quote: In some cases information may be retrieved by personal identifier to facilitate delivery of Consumer Education.
risks.rationale: Searchable identifiers make it easier to locate and link records about a specific person.

risks.description: The system involves transfers between contractor systems and CFPB internal systems, which creates a risk of interception or mishandling during data movement.
risks.evidence_quote: Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated transfers between contractor systems and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels. These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
risks.rationale: Data transfers are a common point of exposure even when encryption is used.

risks.description: The system shares data with external researchers under agreements, but those controls may still leave residual access and disclosure risk.
risks.evidence_quote: When the CFPB collaborates with other researchers, such as those at other federal agencies or academic institutions, legal agreements and non-disclosure agreements are used to restrict access to the data, as appropriate.
risks.rationale: Contractual controls help, but they do not eliminate the risk of downstream misuse or disclosure.

mitigations.description: Adopt and obtain NARA approval for a records disposition schedule as soon as possible, and dispose of records according to the approved schedule.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Records that fall under a general records schedule will be disposed of according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.rationale: A records schedule limits how long personal information is kept and reduces exposure over time.

mitigations.description: Limit collection to only the sensitive fields necessary for the stated purpose and store direct identifiers separately from research data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: In cases where information is necessary for analysis, the direct identifying PII is stored and secured separately.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing and segregating sensitive data reduces the impact of any unauthorized access.

mitigations.description: Require informed consent before any record matching and use de-identified copies of matched datasets for analysis.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Such matching is only conducted subject to the Participant’s informed consent.
mitigations.rationale: Consent and de-identification reduce the privacy impact of combining datasets.

mitigations.description: Use administrative data only when needed for the specific education or evaluation purpose and keep it separated from direct identifiers.
mitigations.evidence_quote: it may at times include Administrative Data regarding an individual’s habits or experiences related to specific financial products or services, such as credit scores, account balances, payment histories.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting use of sensitive financial data lowers the chance of unnecessary exposure.

mitigations.description: Collect website and online tool data in aggregate form and suppress or generalize fields that could enable user tracking.
mitigations.evidence_quote: This information is generally collected in aggregate and is not directly identifying.
mitigations.rationale: Aggregation reduces the ability to link online activity to a specific person.

mitigations.description: Use explicit participant consent and clear notice before collecting information from third parties, and limit third-party data to what is necessary.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Consumer Education primarily relies on information collected directly from the individual and with the individual’s consent to collect information from third parties, such as those that offer or provide consumer financial products or services.
mitigations.rationale: Consent and limitation help participants understand and control third-party collection.

mitigations.description: Continue to avoid sharing response data in un-aggregated form and apply disclosure-protection techniques such as aggregation, rounding, and exclusion of variables or observations.
mitigations.evidence_quote: any products disclosed do not include direct identifying PII, and will typically be subject to further disclosure- protection procedures such as aggregation of response categories, generalized sentiments of Participants, rounding, exclusion of some variables, or exclusion of observations.
mitigations.rationale: Disclosure protection reduces the risk that shared outputs reveal individual-level information.

mitigations.description: Restrict retrieval by personal identifier to staff with a need to know and use it only when necessary for delivering Consumer Education.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB only grants access to the information collected for Consumer Education to CFPB personnel with a need to know.
mitigations.rationale: Need-to-know access reduces the chance that identifiable records are exposed or misused.

mitigations.description: Continue using encrypted tunnels and encrypted email for transfers, and document and review transfer controls in the relevant security plans.
mitigations.evidence_quote: These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
mitigations.rationale: Encryption helps protect data while it is moving between systems.

mitigations.description: Use legal agreements and non-disclosure agreements with external collaborators to restrict access and disclosure, and apply them consistently.
mitigations.evidence_quote: legal agreements and non-disclosure agreements are used to restrict access to the data, as appropriate.
mitigations.rationale: Binding agreements help limit what outside collaborators can do with the data.

risks.description: The CFPB may collect information from people in real-world consumer financial settings, which can expose personal financial behavior and experiences to privacy risk.
risks.evidence_quote: As part of its research programs, the Bureau utilizes primary data collection in the consumer financial market (“Market Research in the Field”).
risks.rationale: Primary data collection in natural settings can involve sensitive consumer information even when the stated purpose is research.

risks.description: The CFPB may share collected information with outside collaborators, creating a risk of broader access beyond the Bureau.
risks.evidence_quote: When conducting Market Research in the Field, the CFPB may collaborate with third parties, including consumer financial products or service providers, innovators, entrepreneurs, non- profit or academic institutions, community-based organizations, or nonprofits; and social science researchers who are active in or may contribute insight into the consumer financial market.
risks.rationale: Sharing information with multiple third parties increases the number of parties that could see or handle personal data.

risks.description: Third-party collaboration can create accountability gaps if roles and responsibilities are not clearly controlled.
risks.evidence_quote: In considering proposals by third parties, the CFPB evaluates whether the proposals align with Bureau research or policy goals or mandates, meet specified standards and procedures, and whether appropriate legal agreements establish roles, responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms.
risks.rationale: The need for legal agreements and accountability mechanisms indicates a risk that third-party handling could otherwise be insufficiently governed.

risks.description: Research participants may not fully understand how their information is used or shared because the system relies on generally applicable notice and consent rather than a specific, detailed disclosure in the context provided.
risks.evidence_quote: Generally applicable: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
risks.rationale: General opportunities for notice and consent may be less protective than a more specific explanation of collection, use, and sharing.

risks.description: The system may retain or process information over a longer period of time because the research can occur over extended periods in natural environments.
risks.evidence_quote: Via Market Research in the Field, the CFPB can evaluate how economic activity operates in naturally occurring environments, and it generally allows for research to occur over a longer period of time than in a lab setting.
risks.rationale: Longer research timelines can increase the amount of time personal information is exposed to misuse or unauthorized access.

risks.description: The system may involve sensitive consumer financial information because it studies consumer awareness, decision-making, experiences, and financial behavior.
risks.evidence_quote: In general, the CFPB designs Market Research in the Field to provide insight into: • Consumer awareness and decision-making, for example, understanding what financial products or features people are aware of and why they choose one product over another; • Consumer experiences and potential risks to consumers, including traditionally underserved consumers, in order to help them improve their financial lives;
risks.rationale: Information about financial choices and experiences can reveal sensitive personal circumstances.

risks.description: Research may involve technologies or product innovation that could collect or reveal additional personal information in ways not fully described here.
risks.evidence_quote: How consumer financial products or services, or their features, can benefit consumers to make consumer financial markets work better for the American people; and • The development or impact of technologies or product innovation.
risks.rationale: Technology-enabled research can expand the types or volume of information collected beyond what is obvious to participants.

mitigations.description: Apply the stated CFPB privacy protections and security controls to all primary data collection and limit collection to the minimum information needed for the research question.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Standard privacy and security controls reduce the chance that collected consumer information is exposed or misused.

mitigations.description: Restrict third-party access to only the data necessary for the approved research task and require data-sharing terms that prohibit secondary use.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting what collaborators receive and how they may use it reduces exposure from external sharing.

mitigations.description: Use written agreements that define each party's responsibilities, security obligations, and accountability mechanisms before any collaboration begins.
mitigations.evidence_quote: appropriate legal agreements establish roles, responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms.
mitigations.rationale: Clear contractual controls help ensure third parties handle information consistently and securely.

mitigations.description: Provide clear, participant-specific notice describing what information is collected, how it will be used, and with whom it may be shared, and obtain informed consent where feasible.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Generally applicable: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
mitigations.rationale: More specific notice and consent improve transparency and help participants make informed choices.

mitigations.description: Set and enforce retention limits tied to the research purpose, and delete or de-identify data when the longer field study is complete.
mitigations.rationale: Retention limits reduce the period during which personal information remains exposed.

mitigations.description: Treat consumer financial behavior and experience data as sensitive and apply heightened access controls, minimization, and de-identification where possible.
mitigations.rationale: Enhanced safeguards are appropriate because the research can reveal sensitive financial circumstances.

mitigations.description: Perform privacy review before using new technologies or product innovations to confirm what data they collect and whether the collection is necessary.
mitigations.rationale: Pre-deployment review helps prevent unexpected collection or disclosure of personal information.

risks.description: Mortgage application and loan data are disclosed to multiple federal agencies, increasing the number of parties that can access sensitive borrower information.
risks.evidence_quote: Appropriate federal agencies are member agencies of the Federal Financial Institutions Examinations Council—the Bu reau, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Board of Gov ernors of the Federal Reserve System, and the National Credit Union Administration —as well as the Department of Housing and Urban Development (collectively, “Federal HMDA agencies”).
risks.rationale: Each additional recipient expands the exposure surface for the reported data.

risks.description: The platform collects detailed HMDA data about originations, purchases, and applications for covered loans, which may include information that is sensitive when linked to a borrower or property.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB will collect HMDA data, from certain financial institutions, that are required by Regulation C regarding originations of, purchases of, and applications for covered loans.
risks.rationale: Loan and application records can reveal financial behavior and housing-related decisions.

risks.description: The system processes data submitted electronically by financial institutions, creating risk of unauthorized access or loss during transmission or submission.
risks.evidence_quote: financial institutions shall submit its loan/application register in electronic format to the appropriate federal agency at the address identified by such agency
risks.rationale: Electronic submission can expose data to interception or mishandling if protections fail.

risks.description: The system is intended to support identification of discriminatory lending patterns, which means the reported data may be used to draw inferences about individuals or groups.
risks.evidence_quote: to assist in identifying possible discriminatory lending patterns and enforcing antidiscrimination statutes.
risks.rationale: Analytical use of detailed lending data can create privacy concerns if results are associated with particular people or neighborhoods.

risks.description: The platform has no public participation component, limiting individuals' ability to correct or challenge information before it is used.
risks.evidence_quote: The HMDA Platform does not have a public participation component.
risks.rationale: Without participation, affected people have fewer opportunities to notice and remedy inaccurate records.

risks.description: The system relies on standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls, but the PIA does not describe any HMDA-specific access restrictions or minimization measures.
risks.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
risks.rationale: A lack of system-specific safeguards can leave detailed mortgage data insufficiently constrained.

mitigations.description: Limit access to HMDA submissions to only those federal agencies and personnel with a documented need to know, and log all inter-agency access.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting access reduces the privacy impact of sharing the data with multiple agencies.

mitigations.description: Apply data minimization by collecting and retaining only the HMDA fields required by Regulation C for the stated reporting purpose.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB will collect HMDA data, from certain financial institutions, that are required by Regulation C regarding originations of, purchases of, and applications for covered loans.
mitigations.rationale: Collecting only required fields limits unnecessary exposure of borrower information.

mitigations.description: Require secure electronic transmission for submissions, such as encrypted file transfer and validation of the submitting institution.
mitigations.rationale: Secure transmission reduces the risk of interception or tampering during electronic submission.

mitigations.description: Use privacy review and aggregation rules before any analytic or disclosure use that could identify individuals or small groups.
mitigations.evidence_quote: to assist in identifying possible discriminatory lending patterns and enforcing antidiscrimination statutes.
mitigations.rationale: Aggregation and review help prevent unintended identification while preserving the policy purpose.

mitigations.description: Provide a correction or dispute process for institutions to fix submitted HMDA records before final use or disclosure.
mitigations.rationale: A review-and-correction path can reduce the privacy and fairness harms of inaccurate data.

mitigations.description: Document HMDA-specific access, retention, and audit controls in addition to the Bureau's standard privacy protections and security controls.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Explicit system-specific controls make it clearer how detailed mortgage data is protected in practice.

risks.description: The system collects and reports age and credit score, which are sensitive personal attributes that can reveal detailed financial and demographic information about borrowers.
risks.evidence_quote: 8 Age and credit score are new data points under the 2015 HMDA Rule. These data will be collected beginning in 2018 and first reported to Federal HMDA agencies, including the CFPB, in 2019.
risks.rationale: Age and credit score are highly revealing data elements, so their collection and reporting increases privacy exposure.

risks.description: The system requires lenders to collect self-identified disaggregated ethnic and racial categories, creating a risk of exposure of highly sensitive demographic data.
risks.evidence_quote: 7 Beginning in 2018, Regulation C will require lenders to permit applicants and borrowers to self-identify u sing disaggregated ethnic and racial categories.
risks.rationale: Race and ethnicity information is sensitive and can be used to infer protected characteristics.

risks.description: HMDA data must be disclosed to the public, creating a risk that borrower-level mortgage information can be widely accessed and linked back to individuals.
risks.evidence_quote: 13 See Regulation C, 12 C.F.R. § 1 003.1(c) (requiring certain financial institutions, including banks, savings associations, credit unions, and other mortgage lending institutions to report data about home purchase loans, home im provement loans, and refinancings that it originates or purchases, or for which it receives applications, and to disclose certain data to the public).
risks.rationale: Public disclosure increases the chance that data will be re-identified or used beyond the original collection purpose.

risks.description: The system collects mortgage application and loan data from covered financial institutions on an annual and, for some institutions, quarterly basis, which increases the volume and frequency of stored personal information and the exposure from unauthorized access or breach.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB will collect HMDA data annually 9 from covered financial institutions that are required to report under Regulation C regarding originations of, purchases of, and applications for covered loans.
risks.rationale: More frequent and broader collection means more records are held and more opportunities exist for compromise.

risks.description: The data are submitted electronically to federal agencies, which creates transmission and centralized storage risks for sensitive mortgage data.
risks.evidence_quote: 21 See Regulation C, Appendix A.II, effective Jan. 1, 2018 (prescribing that a financial institution shall submit its loan/application register in electronic format to the appropriate federal agency at the address identified by such agency).
risks.rationale: Electronic submission and centralized receipt increase the importance of secure transfer and storage controls.

risks.description: The system shares HMDA data with multiple federal agencies, expanding the number of recipients who can access the information.
risks.evidence_quote: 5 Appropriate federal agencies are member agencies of the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council—the Bu reau, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Board of Gov ernors of the Federal Reserve System, and the National Credit Union Administration—as well as the Department of Hou sing and Urban Development (collectively, “Federal HMDA agencies”).
risks.rationale: Each additional recipient increases the risk of misuse, unauthorized disclosure, or inconsistent protection.
