mitigations.description: Apply stronger controls or suppression rules when using sensitive demographic and financial variables for proxying, so outputs cannot be used to infer information about specific individuals or small groups.
mitigations.evidence_quote: When the CFPB collects and uses PII, it does so in order to proxy based on population characteristics;
mitigations.rationale: Limiting sensitive inference helps prevent disclosure through statistical proxying.

mitigations.description: Validate and document external-source data before use, including checks for accuracy, timeliness, and relevance, and correct or exclude records that are clearly unreliable.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Administrative Data is gathered from third parties, commercial sources, and public databases.
mitigations.rationale: Quality checks reduce the chance that inaccurate external data will be used in privacy-impacting ways.

mitigations.description: Provide direct CFPB notice or a public-facing notice about the data sources and research use whenever practicable, rather than relying only on third parties to notify individuals.
mitigations.rationale: Direct notice improves transparency and gives people clearer awareness of how their data is used.

mitigations.description: Adopt and implement a retention schedule as soon as possible, and delete or archive records according to the shortest lawful retention period consistent with research needs.
mitigations.rationale: Shorter retention lowers the amount of time the records remain exposed to privacy risk.

mitigations.description: Review public and external reports for disclosure risk before release, including aggregation thresholds and suppression of small cells or rare combinations that could enable re-identification.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Products of Market Research consist of aggregate information, such as tabulations and statistical results, that are included in internal reports, CFPB whitepapers and studies, and other policy output, and do not contain direct identifying PII.
mitigations.rationale: Disclosure review helps ensure aggregate outputs remain non-identifying in practice.

mitigations.description: Enforce role-based access reviews, logging, and periodic audits for personnel with access to Market Research data, with extra safeguards for highly sensitive fields such as biometric or health information.
mitigations.rationale: Monitoring and auditability reduce the chance of unauthorized insider access.

risks.description: Even without direct identifiers, users may be able to isolate a single loan record and infer details about an individual applicant or borrower from the public dataset. This creates a re-identification or singling-out risk from highly granular loan-level and property data.
risks.evidence_quote: Users may be able to isolate a single record, but the record will not contain any direct identifiers.
risks.rationale: A record that can be isolated can still reveal sensitive facts when combined with other available information.

risks.description: The dataset includes sensitive application and outcome details that could expose financial circumstances, credit behavior, and denial reasons for individual mortgage applicants. Public release of these fields increases the risk of harm from unwanted disclosure.
risks.evidence_quote: The HMDA Public Use Dataset includes the following information: • Loan data o Application year o Loan or application type, purpose, amount (rounded to nearest thousand) o Action taken and denial reason, if applicable o Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act (HOEPA) flag o Lien status (first, subordinate, unsecured) o Rate spread on higher-priced mortgages o Purchaser type o Preapproval request
risks.rationale: These fields can reveal detailed financial and lending outcomes about a household even without names.

risks.description: The dataset includes location information at a fine geographic level, which can make it easier to link a loan record to a specific property or household. This increases the chance of indirect identification in sparsely populated areas or for unusual transactions.
risks.evidence_quote: • Property data o Census tract, Metropolitan Statistical Area or Metropolitan Division, State, County o Property type
risks.rationale: Detailed geography narrows the set of possible individuals associated with a record.

risks.description: Because the public can query, filter, download, and share the dataset, external users can combine records with other sources to re-identify people or profile borrowers. The API also enables reuse in other applications and systems, expanding downstream privacy exposure.
risks.evidence_quote: The data publishing API permits users to create visualizations from the Dataset and to query and filter the Dataset to create custom summary tables. The data publishing API also enables users to download or share data in the Dataset in a variety of formats.
risks.rationale: Broad public re-use makes linkage attacks and secondary use more likely.

risks.description: The CFPB republishes data that it does not independently verify, so any privacy-protective redactions or modifications made upstream could be incomplete or erroneous. If sensitive fields were not properly removed before republication, the public dataset could expose applicant or borrower information.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB accepts the HMDA Public Use Dataset from the FFIEC as accurate and complete, and does not alter the data or independently verify the accuracy and completeness of the dataset before republishing it on consumerfinance.gov.
risks.rationale: Relying on upstream processing without independent review can allow privacy-protective errors to persist.

risks.description: The system retains the public dataset until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA, which may prolong exposure of loan-level information. Longer retention increases the window for misuse, linkage, and repeated access over time.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB will continue to retain these records until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA.
risks.rationale: Keeping public records available for longer increases cumulative privacy risk.

risks.description: Public access is read-only and requires no authorization, so anyone, including federal and state agencies and private sector organizations, can access the dataset without restriction. This broad access increases the likelihood of mass collection and secondary use beyond the original disclosure purpose.
risks.evidence_quote: The public has read-only access to the HMDA Public Use Dataset made available on consumerfinance.gov. There is no authorization process for read- only access to the Dataset.
risks.rationale: Unrestricted access makes broad downstream use and aggregation easier.

risks.description: The dataset may be combined with other public or proprietary information to infer protected characteristics or other sensitive attributes about applicants. The presence of race, ethnicity, and sex notice in the collection context highlights the possibility that the data supports sensitive inferences even if those fields are not listed in the public-use excerpt.
risks.evidence_quote: Lenders are required to inform mortgage applicants that the Federal government requests information concerning the ethnicity, race, and sex of the applicant in order to monitor compliance with Federal statutes that prohibit lenders from discriminating against applicants on these bases.
risks.rationale: Data that supports fair-lending analysis can also enable sensitive profiling when linked with other sources.

mitigations.description: Continue and strengthen de-identification review before publication, including testing whether single records can be isolated in combination with other public data sources.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The information reported to regulators pursuant to HMDA and Regulation C is modified to protect loan applicant privacy and is made available to the public annually on the FFIEC’s website.
mitigations.rationale: Testing for singling-out risk helps ensure the public dataset remains non-identifying.

mitigations.description: Limit publication to the minimum fields needed for public understanding and continue suppressing or rounding fields that could reveal sensitive financial outcomes.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The HMDA Public Use Dataset includes the following information: • Loan data o Application year o Loan or application type, purpose, amount (rounded to nearest thousand) o Action taken and denial reason, if applicable
mitigations.rationale: Reducing precision and limiting sensitive fields lowers the chance of harm from disclosure.

mitigations.description: Apply geographic generalization or suppression where needed to reduce the chance that a record can be tied to a specific household or property.
mitigations.evidence_quote: • Property data o Census tract, Metropolitan Statistical Area or Metropolitan Division, State, County o Property type
mitigations.rationale: Coarser geography makes it harder to identify a specific property or borrower.

mitigations.description: Provide clear reuse guidance and privacy warnings on the API and download pages, including cautions against attempting re-identification or combining the dataset with other sources to identify individuals.
mitigations.rationale: Clear notices can reduce misuse by informing users of the privacy risks of downstream linkage.

mitigations.description: Add a CFPB spot-check or validation step for privacy-protective redactions before republication, especially for fields that could indirectly identify borrowers.
mitigations.rationale: Independent checks would reduce the chance that upstream privacy errors are republished unchanged.

mitigations.description: Adopt and publish a CFPB records retention schedule as soon as possible, and periodically review whether continued retention of the public dataset remains necessary.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB will continue to retain these records until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA.
mitigations.rationale: A defined retention schedule limits unnecessary long-term exposure.

mitigations.description: Keep access read-only for the public and maintain the non-public database layer behind CFPB access controls for operational staff only.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The public has read-only access to the HMDA Public Use Dataset made available on consumerfinance.gov. There is no authorization process for read- only access to the Dataset. Users cannot write to the system. The data publishing API is supported by a non-publicly available database layer that is not accessible by external users.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting write and backend access reduces unauthorized modification and exposure.

mitigations.description: Perform privacy review for sensitive-inference risk before release of any new fields or formats, especially where the data could be combined with other datasets to infer protected characteristics.
mitigations.rationale: Reviewing inference risk helps prevent disclosure of sensitive attributes through linkage.

risks.description: The system collects highly sensitive identifiers and personal data, including SSNs, financial information, biometric information, and health or medical information, which creates a risk of harm if misused or exposed.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB administers, enforces, and implements federal consumer financial protection laws, and, among other powers, has authority to protect consumers from unfair,
risks.rationale: The broader and more sensitive the collected data, the greater the potential impact of unauthorized access or misuse.

risks.description: The system collects sensitive demographic and life-event information that could reveal vulnerable status or protected characteristics when combined with response data.
risks.evidence_quote: Response Data may also contain demographic information, such as race/ethnicity, gender, age, education level, income; and other sensitive information, such as a consumer’s experience with foreclosure or debt collections; existing health condition that impacts access to types of products/services; or status of enrollment in public benefits.
risks.rationale: These fields can expose sensitive attributes and increase the privacy impact of any disclosure or secondary use.

risks.description: The system may create new linked datasets by matching administrative data, credit scores, and response data, increasing the risk of re-identification or expanded profiling.
risks.evidence_quote: In some cases, Consumer Experience Research may involve the matching of records, such as credit score to Response Data, creating new assemblies of information about the Respondent.
risks.rationale: Linking separate datasets can make individuals easier to identify and can reveal more about them than any single source alone.

risks.description: The system may use administrative data to identify survey recipients and to support nonresponse analyses, which can expose individuals to unwanted outreach or profiling based on third-party data.
risks.evidence_quote: In some instances, the CFPB may use Administrative Data collected from a third party to identify potential recipients of surveys, to provide auxiliary information for research, and to support nonresponse analyses.
risks.rationale: Using third-party data for targeting or analysis can affect people who did not directly provide the information for that purpose.

risks.description: The system relies on third-party collection and contractor/vendor transfers, which creates a risk of unauthorized disclosure during sharing or transit.
risks.evidence_quote: Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated data transfers between contractor systems and/or vendor websites and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels. These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
risks.rationale: Data moving among multiple parties and systems has a higher chance of mishandling or interception.

risks.description: Direct identifying PII is retained separately but still stored for scheduling, follow-up, compensation, and matching, creating a risk of unnecessary retention and exposure of identity data.
risks.evidence_quote: When direct identifying PII is necessary to facilitate Consumer Experience Research rather than necessary to the analysis, the direct identifying PII is stored and secured separately.
risks.rationale: Separating identifiers reduces exposure, but retaining them still leaves a target that must be protected.

risks.description: The system may share research products externally, including public dissemination, which could expose sensitive information if disclosure-protection procedures fail or are insufficient.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share products of Consumer Experience Research externally, including by disseminating research results to the general public.
risks.rationale: Public release increases the consequences of any imperfect de-identification or suppression.

risks.description: The system may share direct identifying PII in external products such as case studies or quotes, which risks exposing individuals if consent is incomplete or context changes.
risks.evidence_quote: In some cases where the CPFB seeks to share direct identifying PII in an external product, e.g. case study or quote, the CFBP will obtain consent of the appropriate Respondents prior to disclosure.
risks.rationale: Even with consent, publishing identifiers can reveal identity and associated sensitive experiences.

risks.description: Records are retained indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which creates a risk that personal data will remain available longer than necessary.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Long retention increases the time window for misuse, breach, or secondary use.

mitigations.description: Limit collection of direct identifiers and sensitive fields to only what is necessary for scheduling, follow-up, compensation, or approved analysis, and keep identifiers stored separately from research data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: When direct identifying PII is necessary to facilitate Consumer Experience Research rather than necessary to the analysis, the direct identifying PII is stored and secured separately.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing and separating sensitive data reduces the amount exposed if a breach or misuse occurs.

mitigations.description: Apply disclosure-protection procedures before any release of response data that includes demographic or sensitive information, including aggregation, rounding, variable suppression, and exclusion of observations.
mitigations.evidence_quote: These external products are subject to disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation of response categories, rounding, exclusion of some variables, or exclusion of observations, and typically do not include direct identifying PII.
mitigations.rationale: These techniques reduce the chance that sensitive characteristics can be tied back to a person.

mitigations.description: Use de-identified matched datasets for analysis after matching is complete and keep the linkage keys separate from the research dataset.
mitigations.evidence_quote: After the matching is complete, a de- identified copy of the matched dataset is used for conducting research and analysis.
mitigations.rationale: Removing identifiers from the working dataset lowers re-identification and profiling risk.

mitigations.description: Use administrative data for survey targeting and nonresponse analysis only under documented purpose limits and consent where applicable, and restrict it to the minimum needed fields.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Consumer Experience Research primarily relies on information collected directly from the individual and subject to the individual’s consent for the CFPB to collect additional information from third parties, such as those that offer or provide consumer financial products or services.
mitigations.rationale: Purpose limits and consent help ensure third-party data is used only in ways respondents expect.

mitigations.description: Continue to require encrypted transfers and add strict contractual controls and non-disclosure obligations for contractors, vendors, and collaborating researchers.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated data transfers between contractor systems and/or vendor websites and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels. These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
mitigations.rationale: Encryption and contractual controls reduce the chance of unauthorized access during transfer and sharing.

mitigations.description: Restrict access to direct identifying PII to only staff with a need to know and keep those identifiers secured separately from analysis data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB only grants access to the information collected for Consumer Experience Research to CFPB personnel with a need to know.
mitigations.rationale: Need-to-know access limits exposure of identity data to fewer people.

mitigations.description: Before external publication, apply disclosure-protection review to all research products and remove direct identifiers and other high-risk fields unless disclosure is necessary and authorized.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share products of Consumer Experience Research externally, including by disseminating research results to the general public.
mitigations.rationale: A mandatory review step helps catch residual disclosure risk before public release.

mitigations.description: Require documented, informed consent and a separate approval review before any external product includes a quote, case study, or other direct identifier.
mitigations.evidence_quote: In some cases where the CPFB seeks to share direct identifying PII in an external product, e.g. case study or quote, the CFBP will obtain consent of the appropriate Respondents prior to disclosure.
mitigations.rationale: Explicit consent and review reduce the risk of publishing identifying information without authorization.

mitigations.description: Adopt and implement a records disposition schedule as soon as possible and purge records according to the approved schedule instead of retaining them indefinitely.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
mitigations.rationale: Timely disposal limits how long personal data remains exposed to breach or misuse.

risks.description: The system may include highly sensitive identifiers and personal data, creating a risk of re-identification or misuse if exposed. The PIA says direct identifiers can sometimes be present, including SSNs, financial account numbers, home addresses, and email addresses.
risks.evidence_quote: In some cases, they may include direct identifying PII, including: • Name • Phone number • Home address • Email • Financial account number • Social Security number
risks.rationale: Sensitive identifiers materially increase harm if the data are disclosed or linked back to individuals.

risks.description: The system may collect biometric and health or medical information, which is especially sensitive and could cause significant harm if improperly disclosed or analyzed. The overview explicitly lists these categories among the information included in the system.
risks.evidence_quote: Other Information (including biometric information and health or medical information)
risks.rationale: Highly sensitive data requires stronger controls because misuse can lead to serious privacy and discrimination harms.

risks.description: Individuals generally are not notified when their information is collected or shared, limiting transparency and their ability to understand or challenge use of their data. The PIA says notice is generally not provided in supervisory or enforcement contexts.
risks.evidence_quote: individuals generally will not receive notice that the information is being requested and therefore how such information will be used or disclosed
risks.rationale: Lack of notice reduces individual control and makes privacy harms less visible to affected people.

risks.description: The CFPB may combine records across datasets and create new data about individuals, which can expand what is known about them beyond the original source. The system explicitly uses direct identifying PII to match across datasets and update records.
risks.evidence_quote: When the CFPB does use direct identifying PII in analyses, it does so in order to a) match across datasets; b) update data sets;
risks.rationale: Linking datasets can increase the risk of inaccurate profiling and broaden the privacy impact of each data source.

risks.description: The CFPB may contact potential survey recipients using direct identifying information, which can reveal that a person is associated with a supervision, enforcement, or market research inquiry. The PIA states direct identifying PII may be used to contact potential recipients of surveys.
risks.evidence_quote: contact potential recipients of surveys and then use those surveys to solicit information on consumer experiences with consumer financial products and services.
risks.rationale: Contacting people based on these records can expose their relationship to sensitive financial oversight activity.

risks.description: The system retains records indefinitely until a NARA disposition schedule is approved, which increases the chance of long-term exposure, secondary use, or stale data remaining accessible. The retention section states the CFPB maintains records indefinitely for now.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Long retention generally increases privacy risk because data remain available for misuse or breach over a longer period.

risks.description: Products of market research may be shared with the general public and federal financial regulators, creating a risk that aggregate outputs could still reveal sensitive information if not carefully suppressed. The PIA says these products are shared externally.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share the products of Market Research with the general public and federal financial regulators.
risks.rationale: Even non-identifying outputs can sometimes be re-identified or infer sensitive facts when datasets are small or detailed.

risks.description: Access is limited to CFPB personnel with a need to know, but the system still depends on internal access controls to prevent unauthorized viewing or use of sensitive SEFL Data. The PIA indicates personnel access to the data is granted.
risks.evidence_quote: Only CFPB personnel with a need to know are granted access to SEFL Data used for Market Research.
risks.rationale: Need-to-know access reduces exposure, but any internal access pathway can still be misused without strong controls and monitoring.

mitigations.description: Minimize and mask direct identifiers before analysis, and use de-identified copies whenever possible.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Typically, direct identifying PII has been stripped from SEFL Data used for Market Research.
mitigations.rationale: Removing direct identifiers reduces the chance that records can be tied back to specific people.

mitigations.description: Apply heightened handling controls and strict minimization for biometric and health or medical information, including limiting access to only cases where such data are essential.
mitigations.rationale: Extra safeguards are appropriate because the system includes especially sensitive categories of data.

mitigations.description: Provide notice whenever feasible and, where direct notice is not possible, maintain clear constructive notice describing collection, use, and disclosure practices.
mitigations.evidence_quote: In cases where notice cannot be provided or is not required, the CFPB has provided constructive notice of how it may use such information through this PIA.
mitigations.rationale: Transparency helps affected people understand how their information may be used even when direct notice is unavailable.

mitigations.description: Use record matching only when necessary, and require validation checks before and after linkage to reduce incorrect joins and unintended profiling.
mitigations.evidence_quote: When the CFPB does use direct identifying PII in analyses, it does so in order to a) match across datasets; b) update data sets;
mitigations.rationale: Controls around linkage reduce the risk that merged records create inaccurate or excessive data about individuals.

mitigations.description: Limit survey outreach to the minimum necessary contact information and separate outreach lists from analytic datasets after contact is complete.
mitigations.evidence_quote: contact potential recipients of surveys and then use those surveys to solicit information on consumer experiences with consumer financial products and services.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting outreach data reduces the chance that contact activity exposes sensitive associations.

mitigations.description: Establish and implement a records disposition schedule as soon as practicable, with periodic reviews to dispose of records that are no longer needed.
mitigations.rationale: A defined retention limit lowers the amount of time sensitive records remain exposed to risk.

mitigations.description: Review all public and regulator-facing outputs for disclosure risk before release, including suppression or aggregation of small cells and other potentially identifying details.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB may share the products of Market Research with the general public and federal financial regulators.
mitigations.rationale: Pre-release review helps ensure that aggregate outputs do not inadvertently reveal sensitive information.

mitigations.description: Enforce role-based access controls, logging, and periodic access reviews for all personnel who can reach SEFL Data used for Market Research.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Only CFPB personnel with a need to know are granted access to SEFL Data used for Market Research.
mitigations.rationale: Strong access governance helps ensure that only authorized staff can view or use the data.

risks.description: The system collects highly sensitive personal data, including Social Security numbers, financial information, and even biometric or health information, which could cause significant harm if misused or exposed.
risks.evidence_quote: PROJECT/SYSTEM INCLUDES: Name and other biographic information (e.g. date of birth) Contact Information (address, zip code, telephone number, email address) Social Security number (SSN) or other identifier Financial Information User and Online Information Third Party Information Other Information (including biometric information and health or medical information)
risks.rationale: The broader and more sensitive the collected data, the greater the privacy impact if it is improperly accessed or disclosed.

risks.description: The system may retrieve information by personal identifier, which increases the risk of re-identifying participants and linking their responses to their identity.
risks.evidence_quote: In some cases information may be retrieved by personal identifier to facilitate delivery of Consumer Education.
risks.rationale: Retrieval by identifier makes it easier to associate records with a specific person.

risks.description: The system can match response data with administrative data such as credit scores, balances, payment histories, and other product-use information, creating new information about participants and increasing the sensitivity of the combined profile.
risks.evidence_quote: In some special cases, Consumer Education may involve the matching of records, such as credit score to Response Data, creating new information about the Participant. For example, CFPB may use Administrative Data to evaluate specific consumer education strategies.
risks.rationale: Combining datasets can reveal more about a person than either dataset alone.

risks.description: The system collects website and online tool usage data, including IP address and visit timestamps, which can enable tracking of participant behavior across sessions or services.
risks.evidence_quote: The Bureau may also collect some information related to the use of its website and online tools – specifically how visitors are using the website or tools (including IP address, visit timestamps, browser version and operating system, pages viewed, time on the site, the day and time of access, and the address that linked the user directly to the website or tool) in aggregate form
risks.rationale: Online activity data can still be privacy-sensitive because it may reveal usage patterns and device characteristics.

risks.description: The system relies on information collected from third parties, so participants may have less visibility into what is shared and how it is used.
risks.evidence_quote: Consumer Education primarily relies on information collected directly from the individual and with the individual’s consent to collect information from third parties, such as those that offer or provide consumer financial products or services.
risks.rationale: Third-party collection can reduce individual control and understanding of the data flow.

risks.description: The system may share response data or products with the general public, which could expose participant information if de-identification is incomplete or re-identification becomes possible.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may also share the products of Consumer Education or Response Data with the general public, but any products disclosed do not include direct identifying PII, and will typically be subject to further disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation of response categories, generalized sentiments of Participants, rounding, exclusion of some variables, or exclusion of observations.
risks.rationale: Public disclosure increases the risk that individuals could be indirectly identified from the released content.

risks.description: The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which can prolong exposure and increase the chance of unauthorized access over time.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB maintains computer and paper records indefinitely until the National Archives and Records Administration (“NARA”) approves the CFPB’s records disposition schedule.
risks.rationale: Longer retention generally increases the window in which data can be compromised or misused.

risks.description: The system shares data through non-automated transfers and encrypted email, which can create operational handling risks if transfer procedures are not tightly controlled.
risks.evidence_quote: Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated transfers between contractor systems and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels. These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
risks.rationale: Manual transfer processes are more prone to handling errors than fully automated controls.

mitigations.description: Limit collection to only the minimum sensitive data needed for the specific Consumer Education purpose and keep direct identifiers separated from response and administrative data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: information collected is limited to only that which is necessary to recruit or schedule Participants in Consumer Education, or establish a basis for comparison in evaluating the effectiveness of specific Consumer Education. In cases where information is necessary for analysis, the direct identifying PII is stored and secured separately.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing and segregating sensitive data reduces the amount of information exposed if records are accessed improperly.

mitigations.description: Restrict retrieval by personal identifier to cases where it is necessary for delivery of Consumer Education and maintain the separation of identifying data from research data.
mitigations.evidence_quote: In some cases information may be retrieved by personal identifier to facilitate delivery of Consumer Education. Research on the effectiveness of Consumer Education however, does not rely on direct identifying PII for analysis.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting identifier-based retrieval lowers the chance that identities will be unnecessarily linked to participant records.

mitigations.description: Require informed consent before any record matching and use a de-identified copy of the matched dataset for research and analysis.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Such matching is only conducted subject to the Participant’s informed consent. After the matching is complete, a de-identified copy of the matched dataset is used for conducting research and analysis.
mitigations.rationale: Consent and de-identification reduce the privacy impact of combining datasets.

mitigations.description: Continue collecting website and online tool data in aggregate form and avoid direct identification in analytics outputs.
mitigations.evidence_quote: This information is generally collected in aggregate and is not directly identifying.
mitigations.rationale: Aggregation reduces the likelihood that online usage data can be tied to a specific person.

mitigations.description: Obtain the individual’s consent before collecting information from third parties and document those disclosures clearly.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Consumer Education primarily relies on information collected directly from the individual and with the individual’s consent to collect information from third parties
mitigations.rationale: Consent helps ensure individuals know when outside entities are contributing information about them.

mitigations.description: Apply disclosure-protection techniques such as aggregation, rounding, exclusion of variables, and exclusion of observations before any public release.
mitigations.evidence_quote: will typically be subject to further disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation of response categories, generalized sentiments of Participants, rounding, exclusion of some variables, or exclusion of observations.
mitigations.rationale: These techniques reduce the chance that public products can be linked back to individuals.

mitigations.description: Finalize and implement a NARA-approved records disposition schedule so records are not retained longer than necessary.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The CFPB will continue to retain these records until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA. Records that fall under a general records schedule will be disposed of according to the applicable schedule.
mitigations.rationale: A disposition schedule creates a defined retention limit and reduces unnecessary long-term exposure.

mitigations.description: Continue using encrypted tunnels and encrypted email for transfers and add strict handling controls for non-automated transfers.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Any system interactions are pushed, non-automated transfers between contractor systems and CFPB internal systems, which take place via encrypted tunnels. These transfers can also take place via an encrypted email client.
mitigations.rationale: Encryption and controlled transfer procedures help protect data during movement between systems.

risks.description: The CFPB may collect information from people in real-world settings over a longer period of time, which can create a risk of broader exposure of consumer information than a one-time transaction would.
risks.evidence_quote: Via Market Research in the Field, the CFPB can evaluate how economic activity operates in naturally occurring environments, and it generally allows for research to occur over a longer period of time than in a lab setting.
risks.rationale: Longer-duration field research can increase the amount of personal information observed or retained.

risks.description: The CFPB may share or receive consumer information through collaborations with third parties, creating a risk that data will be disclosed beyond the Bureau.
risks.evidence_quote: When conducting Market Research in the Field, the CFPB may collaborate with third parties, including consumer financial products or service providers, innovators, entrepreneurs, non- profit or academic institutions, community-based organizations, or nonprofits; and social science researchers who are active in or may contribute insight into the consumer financial market.
risks.rationale: Third-party collaboration expands the number of entities that may access sensitive consumer information.

risks.description: The system may involve contractors or third-party collaborators handling the information, which increases the risk of unauthorized use or disclosure if roles are not tightly controlled.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB may lead Market Research in the Field directly, contract with a third party, or accept a collaboration proposal submitted by a third party.
risks.rationale: More parties handling the data increases the chance of inconsistent privacy and security practices.

risks.description: The system may use primary data collection in consumer financial markets, which can capture information from individuals who may not expect research collection in everyday market activity.
risks.evidence_quote: As part of its research programs, the Bureau utilizes primary data collection in the consumer financial market (“Market Research in the Field”).
risks.rationale: Collecting data directly in the field can reduce individuals' awareness of when and how their information is being gathered.

risks.description: The system may collect information about consumer awareness, decision-making, experiences, and risks, which can be sensitive because it reveals financial behavior and vulnerabilities.
risks.evidence_quote: In general, the CFPB designs Market Research in the Field to provide insight into: • Consumer awareness and decision-making, for example, understanding what financial products or features people are aware of and why they choose one product over another; • Consumer experiences and potential risks to consumers, including traditionally underserved consumers, in order to help them improve their financial lives;
risks.rationale: Information about financial choices and risks can reveal personal circumstances that merit protection.

risks.description: The system may collect information about the effect of disclosures, education, and technology on consumer behavior, which can enable profiling or inference about individuals' financial behavior.
risks.evidence_quote: • Information disclosure and how disclosure may affect behavior; • The effect of educational or other interventions on consumer financial behavior or outcomes; • How consumer financial products or services, or their features, can benefit consumers to make consumer financial markets work better for the American people; and • The development or impact of technologies or product innovation.
risks.rationale: Behavioral research data can be used to infer preferences, responsiveness, or other personal traits.

risks.description: The system relies on standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls, but the input does not describe any field-specific limits on access, sharing, or retention, leaving a residual risk of over-collection or over-retention.
risks.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
risks.rationale: General controls may not fully address risks unique to field research without additional system-specific safeguards.

risks.description: The input says there are generally applicable opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress, which implies participation may not always be individualized or fully informed in every case.
risks.evidence_quote: Generally applicable: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
risks.rationale: Broadly described participation rights may not ensure that each affected person understands and can control the collection.

mitigations.description: Minimize collection and retention to only the data needed for the specific research question, and de-identify or aggregate data as early as possible.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing the amount and identifiability of data lowers the privacy impact of longer-term field research.

mitigations.description: Use written data-sharing agreements that limit third-party access, prohibit secondary use, and require privacy and security controls for any collaborator.
mitigations.evidence_quote: the CFPB evaluates whether the proposals align with Bureau research or policy goals or mandates, meet specified standards and procedures, and whether appropriate legal agreements establish roles, responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms.
mitigations.rationale: Formal agreements can constrain how collaborators use and protect shared information.

mitigations.description: Require role-based access controls and explicit handling instructions for contractors and third parties, with oversight and auditability.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting access by role and monitoring handling reduces the chance of misuse by outside parties.

mitigations.description: Provide clear notice to participants before or at the point of collection about what data is being collected, why it is being collected, and how it will be used.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Generally applicable: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
mitigations.rationale: Notice helps individuals understand field data collection that occurs in ordinary market settings.

mitigations.description: Limit the collection of sensitive financial behavior details to what is necessary and, where possible, use aggregated analysis instead of individual-level reporting.
mitigations.rationale: Collecting and reporting less granular behavioral information reduces the sensitivity of the dataset.

mitigations.description: Apply privacy review to any analysis that infers behavior or outcomes, and suppress outputs that could identify or unfairly characterize individuals.
mitigations.rationale: Reviewing inference-based analysis helps prevent unnecessary disclosure of personal behavioral profiles.

mitigations.description: Publish system-specific privacy and retention limits for field research rather than relying only on general CFPB controls.
mitigations.rationale: Specific limits make it clearer how the Bureau will constrain collection, use, and retention for this research.

mitigations.description: Ensure participants receive meaningful consent and access/redress processes tailored to the field research setting.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Generally applicable: Appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress.
mitigations.rationale: Tailored participation rights improve transparency and individual control in research contexts.

risks.description: The platform collects detailed mortgage application and loan data from financial institutions, which can expose sensitive consumer financial and housing information if mishandled.
risks.evidence_quote: The CFPB will collect HMDA data, from certain financial institutions, that are required by Regulation C regarding originations of, purchases of, and applications for covered loans.
risks.rationale: Mortgage data can reveal highly sensitive information about a person’s financial behavior and housing activity.

risks.description: The system receives data from multiple financial institutions and agencies, increasing the chance that information could be shared more broadly than intended.
risks.evidence_quote: The HMDA Platform does not have a public participation component.
risks.rationale: When a system is used for reporting across institutions, privacy risk increases if access and sharing are not tightly controlled.

risks.description: Because the data are used to identify possible discriminatory lending patterns and enforce antidiscrimination statutes, individuals may be subject to profiling or adverse attention based on their mortgage records.
risks.evidence_quote: The data- related requirements in HMDA and Regulation C serve three primary purposes: ... (3) to assist in identifying possible discriminatory lending patterns and enforcing antidiscrimination statutes.
risks.rationale: Analytical use of mortgage records can create privacy concerns if individuals are singled out from pattern detection.

risks.description: The platform supports reporting of information that will be disclosed to the public under Regulation C, creating a risk that personal information becomes publicly accessible.
risks.evidence_quote: See also 81 Fed. Reg. 93580 (Dec. 21, 2016) (establishing current $44 million asset threshold for for data collected in 2017).
risks.rationale: Public disclosure of mortgage data can reduce individuals’ control over information tied to their borrowing and housing choices.

risks.description: The system depends on electronic submission of loan/application registers, which creates a risk of unauthorized access or interception during transmission or storage.
risks.evidence_quote: a financial institution shall submit its loan/application register in electronic format to the appropriate federal agency
risks.rationale: Electronic submission expands the attack surface for privacy breaches if transport and storage protections fail.

risks.description: The data are collected by and shared among several federal HMDA agencies, so a broader set of recipients may increase the number of points where privacy controls could fail.
risks.evidence_quote: Appropriate federal agencies are member agencies of the Federal Financial Institutions Examinations Council—the Bu reau, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Board of Gov ernors of the Federal Reserve System, and the National Credit Union Administration —as well as the Department of Housing and Urban Development (collectively, “Federal HMDA agencies”).
risks.rationale: More recipients generally means more opportunities for unauthorized disclosure or inconsistent safeguards.

mitigations.description: Limit access to HMDA data to authorized personnel only and apply standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting access and applying security controls reduces the chance that sensitive mortgage data are mishandled.

mitigations.description: Use role-based access controls and sharing restrictions so only authorized users and agencies can view the data they need.
mitigations.rationale: Tight access and sharing limits reduce the likelihood of broader-than-intended disclosure across institutions.

mitigations.description: Minimize the data used for analysis and reporting to only what is necessary for HMDA purposes.
mitigations.rationale: Data minimization lowers the risk that individuals are unnecessarily profiled from mortgage records.

mitigations.description: Apply disclosure review and suppress or aggregate fields before any public release of HMDA data.
mitigations.rationale: Reviewing disclosures before release helps prevent public exposure of information that could identify individuals.

mitigations.description: Encrypt electronic submissions and stored loan/application registers.
mitigations.rationale: Encryption helps protect data from interception or unauthorized access during transmission and storage.

mitigations.description: Require consistent privacy and security requirements across all Federal HMDA agencies that receive the data.
mitigations.rationale: Uniform controls across recipients reduce the chance that one recipient becomes the weak point in the handling chain.

risks.description: The system collects and reports sensitive mortgage data, including age, credit score, and self-identified race and ethnicity, which could expose applicants to privacy harm if mishandled or disclosed too broadly.
risks.evidence_quote:
8 Age and credit score are new data points under the 2015 HMDA Rule. These data will be collected beginning in 2018 and first reported to Federal HMDA agencies, including the CFPB, in 2019.
7 Beginning in 2018, Regulation C will require lenders to permit applicants and borrowers to self-identify u sing disaggregated ethnic and racial categories.
risks.rationale: These data elements are personally sensitive and can reveal financial status and protected-class information.

risks.description: The system requires annual and, for some institutions, quarterly submission of HMDA data, increasing the volume and frequency of transfers and the chance of unauthorized access or disclosure.
risks.evidence_quote:
The CFPB will collect HMDA data annually 9 from covered financial institutions that are required to report under Regulation C regarding originations of, purchases of, and applications for covered loans.
9 Beginning in 2020, larger covered financial institutions will submit HMDA data on a quarterly basis.
risks.rationale: More frequent reporting creates more opportunities for data exposure during transmission and processing.

risks.description: The data are disclosed to the public, which can create a re-identification risk even though HMDA does not require direct identifiers.
risks.evidence_quote: requiring certain financial institutions, including banks, savings associations, credit unions, and other mortgage lending institutions to report data about home purchase loans, home im provement loans, and refinancings that it originates or purchases, or for which it receives applications, and to disclose certain data to the public
risks.rationale: Public release of detailed loan data can allow individuals to be inferred from combinations of attributes.

risks.description: Although direct identifiers are not required, institutions may still include them in identification numbers or submissions, which could directly identify applicants or borrowers.
risks.evidence_quote: HMDA does not require the reporting of PII that directly identifies an applicant or borrower, and staff commentary to Regulation C applicable to data collected in 2017 strongly discourages institutions from including in identification numbers names or social security numbers, which are direct identifiers.
risks.rationale: If direct identifiers are included, the dataset becomes much more revealing and easier to misuse.

risks.description: The CFPB receives data from many covered financial institutions and multiple federal agencies, expanding the number of entities that handle the information and the risk of inconsistent safeguards.
risks.evidence_quote: Appropriate federal agencies are member agencies of the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council—the Bu reau, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Board of Gov ernors of the Federal Reserve System, and the National Credit Union Administration—as well as the Department of Hou sing and Urban Development (collectively, “Federal HMDA agencies”).
risks.rationale: More recipients and handlers generally increase the attack surface and the chance of mishandling.

risks.description: Loan/application registers are submitted electronically, which creates a risk of interception, unauthorized access, or transmission errors during submission.
risks.evidence_quote: prescribing that a financial institution shall submit its loan/application register in electronic format to the appropriate federal agency at the address identified by such agency
risks.rationale: Electronic submission requires strong transport and endpoint protections to prevent exposure in transit.

mitigations.description: Apply strict access controls, minimization, and security protections to sensitive fields such as age, credit score, race, and ethnicity, and limit use to authorized HMDA purposes.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: The PIA already states that standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply, which should reduce the risk from sensitive data handling.

mitigations.description: Use secure transmission, validation, and monitoring controls for annual and quarterly submissions, with heightened review for high-volume filers.
mitigations.evidence_quote:
The CFPB will collect HMDA data annually 9 from covered financial institutions that are required to report under Regulation C regarding originations of, purchases of, and applications for covered loans.
9 Beginning in 2020, larger covered financial institutions will submit HMDA data on a quarterly basis.
mitigations.rationale: More frequent submissions justify stronger transfer and monitoring controls to reduce exposure risk.

mitigations.description: Limit public disclosure to the minimum data elements required and apply disclosure review or suppression rules to reduce re-identification risk.
mitigations.evidence_quote: requiring certain financial institutions, including banks, savings associations, credit unions, and other mortgage lending institutions to report data about home purchase loans, home im provement loans, and refinancings that it originates or purchases, or for which it receives applications, and to disclose certain data to the public
mitigations.rationale: Public release should be narrowed where possible to reduce the chance that individuals can be inferred from the data.

mitigations.description: Continue to prohibit direct identifiers in HMDA submissions and validate incoming files to detect names, Social Security numbers, or similar identifiers before acceptance.
mitigations.evidence_quote: HMDA does not require the reporting of PII that directly identifies an applicant or borrower, and staff commentary to Regulation C applicable to data collected in 2017 strongly discourages institutions from including in identification numbers names or social security numbers, which are direct identifiers.
mitigations.rationale: The input already discourages direct identifiers, and validation would enforce that expectation.

mitigations.description: Apply consistent privacy and security controls across all Federal HMDA agencies that receive the data, including role-based access and sharing restrictions.
mitigations.evidence_quote: Yes, all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Consistent controls across all recipients reduce the risk created by multiple handling entities.

mitigations.description: Require encrypted electronic submission and secure agency endpoints for loan/application registers.
mitigations.evidence_quote: prescribing that a financial institution shall submit its loan/application register in electronic format to the appropriate federal agency at the address identified by such agency
mitigations.rationale: Electronic filing should be protected against interception and unauthorized access in transit.

risks.description: The tool collects contact PII from regulated entities, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse of names, phone numbers, and email addresses. Even though the collection is voluntary, the system still stores identifiable contact information for onboarding and assessment submission.
risks.evidence_quote: The OMWI Diversity Assessment Tool contains information to include the PII of contacts for the submitting financial entities
risks.rationale: Collecting identifiable contact data increases the impact if access controls fail or the data is exposed.

risks.description: Free-text assessment responses and attachments may contain additional personal information beyond the limited contact fields, increasing the chance of over-collection and accidental disclosure. Because the content is optional and open-ended, submitters may include more PII than intended.
risks.evidence_quote: any PII included in free text responses or attachments to a submitted assessment
risks.rationale: Open-ended fields are harder to control and can capture more personal information than the system’s structured fields.

risks.description: The system captures Bureau employee and contractor information, which creates a risk of internal personnel data exposure if the imported identity data is accessed inappropriately. This includes work contact details and organizational information.
risks.evidence_quote: some information about employees and contractors working for the Bureau will be captured when it is imported into the system through Sailpoint
risks.rationale: Imported staff records expand the set of personal data stored in the tool and therefore the exposure surface.

risks.description: Entity contacts must submit PII to be onboarded, so there is a risk that access to the system depends on providing personal information that may be more than necessary for the assessment itself. The onboarding step could also create a larger repository of contact data than users expect.
risks.evidence_quote: The PII pertaining to an entity contact is collected when the contact is onboarded to gain access to the system.
risks.rationale: Requiring PII for access can increase collection and retention of personal data beyond the core assessment purpose.

risks.description: Aggregated data used for reporting and analytics could still reveal sensitive information if the aggregation is too granular or if small groups are identifiable. Internal dashboards can increase the chance of re-identification or secondary use beyond the original submission context.
risks.evidence_quote: Aggregated data from the tool will be used in an annual report to Congress as well as to create internal dashboards for data analytics.
risks.rationale: Aggregation reduces but does not eliminate privacy risk, especially when data is used in multiple reporting contexts.

mitigations.description: Restrict access to contact PII to only authorized staff with a need to know and apply standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls.
mitigations.evidence_quote: all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply
mitigations.rationale: Limiting access and applying security controls reduces the likelihood of unauthorized disclosure.

mitigations.description: Add validation, warning text, and reviewer procedures to discourage submission of unnecessary personal information in free-text fields and attachments.
mitigations.rationale: Guidance and review can reduce over-collection in open-ended responses.

mitigations.description: Limit imported Bureau employee and contractor data to the minimum needed for system administration and protect it under the same access controls as other PII.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing imported staff data lowers the amount of internal personal information exposed if the system is accessed improperly.

mitigations.description: Collect only the specific onboarding fields needed for access and clearly explain why each PII element is required before submission.
mitigations.rationale: Purpose-limiting onboarding collection helps avoid unnecessary accumulation of personal data.

mitigations.description: Apply disclosure review and aggregation thresholds before using data in the annual report and dashboards to reduce the risk of re-identification.
mitigations.rationale: Reviewing outputs before publication or internal analytics helps prevent small-group identification from aggregated data.

risks.description: The system stores and processes personally identifiable information about requestors, Bureau staff, and other people in request files and generated documents, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal data.
risks.evidence_quote: Documents retrieved in response to a request and documents generated during the request’s processing may contain PII about the individual requestor, Bureau staff, and others.
risks.rationale: A system that handles PII across request records and generated documents can expose multiple individuals if access controls fail.

risks.description: The public-facing portal allows requestors to create accounts, submit requests, access requested records, and communicate with the Bureau, which creates a risk of account compromise or unauthorized access to request materials.
risks.evidence_quote: The FOIAXpress Public Access Link (PAL) is a secure public-facing web portal that leverages Login.gov to provide the public with a single access point for requestors to create individual accounts, submit requests, access requested records and communicate with the Bureau about the status of a request.
risks.rationale: Any account-based portal that exposes records and communications increases the impact of credential theft or unauthorized login.

risks.description: Using a third-party vendor-created system and an external identity service introduces a risk that personal data could be exposed through inter-system integration or vendor handling.
risks.evidence_quote: FOIAXpress is a third-party vendor-created tracking and management software
risks.rationale: When personal data moves through third-party components, the privacy risk depends on the security and data handling of those external services.

risks.description: The same process is used for Privacy Act requests and FOIA requests, which creates a risk that records about a person could be processed or disclosed in a way that is broader than intended for a self-request.
risks.evidence_quote: The Bureau uses the same process for submitting both Privacy Act requests and FOIA requests.
risks.rationale: Combining request types can increase the chance that records are routed or disclosed under the wrong framework.

risks.description: The system supports the full lifecycle of requests, so request-related information may be retained and accumulated over time, increasing the amount of personal data available in one place.
risks.evidence_quote: supports the Bureau in administering the entire lifecycle of FOIA and Privacy Act requests.
risks.rationale: A lifecycle management system can concentrate sensitive information, making any breach or misuse more consequential.

mitigations.description: Apply strong role-based access controls, least-privilege permissions, and logging for all request records and generated documents containing PII.
mitigations.evidence_quote: all standard Bureau privacy protections and security controls apply.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting and auditing access reduces the chance that PII about requestors, staff, or others is disclosed improperly.

mitigations.description: Require multi-factor authentication and session protections for PAL accounts and restrict access to records and communications to authenticated requestors only.
mitigations.rationale: Stronger authentication lowers the risk that an attacker can use a stolen account to view records or messages.

mitigations.description: Use a formal vendor risk-management process for FOIAXpress and Login.gov integration, including security reviews, data-sharing limits, and contractual privacy requirements.
mitigations.rationale: Vendor oversight helps ensure external services handle request data consistently with Bureau privacy expectations.

mitigations.description: Provide workflow checks that distinguish Privacy Act requests from FOIA requests and train staff to route and release records under the correct process.
mitigations.rationale: Clear classification and staff review reduce the chance of processing or disclosure under the wrong request type.

mitigations.description: Minimize retention of request data to the shortest period needed for legal and operational purposes and regularly purge inactive records.
mitigations.rationale: Reducing how long records are kept lowers the volume of personal data exposed if the system is compromised.

risks.description: The system stores inquiry records in a third-party hosted cloud application, which creates a risk of unauthorized access or disclosure by the hosting provider or through the cloud environment.
risks.evidence_quote: Entellitrak is an enterprise level commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) product hosted by a third party service provider
risks.rationale: Third-party hosting expands the number of parties and technical layers that must be secured to protect the information.

risks.description: The system collects and retains personally identifiable information about inquirers, including names tied to summaries of their issues, which could expose sensitive concerns if the record is breached or misused.
risks.evidence_quote: the Office creates an inquiry record in Entellitrak that includes the inquirer’s first and last name, if an individual chooses to provide it, along with a summary of the inquiry.
risks.rationale: Names linked to inquiry summaries can identify individuals and reveal the fact that they contacted the Ombudsman about a problem.

risks.description: Even when contact details are kept outside the system, the office still maintains them in original email, mail, or voicemail formats, which creates additional exposure points for personal information.
risks.evidence_quote: Rather the Ombudsman’s Office maintains contact information separately in the original format submitted by the inquirer (i.e., in the general Ombudsman Office email box, postal mail, or notes taken from the voicemail received).
risks.rationale: Separating contact information does not eliminate risk if those original channels are not equally protected and controlled.

risks.description: The system supports analysis and outreach activities, which could lead to use of inquiry information beyond the original purpose if internal controls are weak.
risks.evidence_quote: Entellitrak also provides the Ombudsman’s Office with the ability to manage its independent outreach activity in an electronic format.
risks.rationale: A system that supports both case management and outreach can increase the chance of secondary use if access and purpose limits are not enforced.

risks.description: Because the system is used to collect, track, manage, process, and analyze inquiry information, there is a risk of overcollection or retention of more information than is needed for the Ombudsman’s mission.
risks.evidence_quote: provides the Ombudsman’s Office with an integrated case management system with functionality to collect, track, manage and, process, as well as analyze information on individual inquiries to the Office.
risks.rationale: Systems with broad processing capabilities can accumulate unnecessary data unless collection is tightly limited.

risks.description: The system may expose information through administrative or development activities if privacy controls are not consistently applied during changes and security reviews.
risks.evidence_quote: system change requests and security assessment and authorization (SA&A) documentation address privacy relative to systems development
risks.rationale: Change management and development processes can introduce privacy risk if they are not carefully controlled.

risks.description: Although the Office says it preserves confidentiality, the system still creates records about people contacting a federal office, which could chill participation if confidentiality is not maintained.
risks.evidence_quote: The Ombudsman’s Office also provides notice on its webpage that it has safeguards in place to preserve confidentiality.
risks.rationale: People may be deterred from seeking help if they fear their inquiry will not remain confidential.

mitigations.description: Require strong vendor security controls, contractual privacy requirements, and regular oversight of the third-party host.
mitigations.evidence_quote: all standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls apply
mitigations.rationale: Applying and monitoring strong controls reduces the risk created by third-party cloud hosting.

mitigations.description: Limit the inquiry record to only the minimum PII needed and continue allowing anonymous submissions when possible.
mitigations.evidence_quote: If the inquirer wishes to remain anonymous, the Office creates a record in Entellitrak without the name of the inquirer, reflecting only a summary of the inquiry.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing identifying information reduces the impact of any unauthorized disclosure.

mitigations.description: Protect the separate email, mail, and voicemail sources with the same access controls, handling rules, and retention limits used for the system record.
mitigations.rationale: The contact information remains sensitive even when stored outside Entellitrak, so those source channels need equivalent safeguards.

mitigations.description: Enforce role-based access and purpose-based use restrictions so outreach and case information can be used only for authorized Ombudsman functions.
mitigations.evidence_quote: used to create and track inquiries to the office and outreach activities
mitigations.rationale: Restricting use to defined purposes helps prevent secondary use of inquiry information.

mitigations.description: Apply data minimization and retention limits so the system keeps only the information needed to manage the inquiry and outreach activity.
mitigations.rationale: Limiting stored data lowers the amount of personal information exposed if the system is compromised.

mitigations.description: Continue requiring privacy review and security authorization for system changes before deployment.
mitigations.evidence_quote: system change requests and security assessment and authorization (SA&A) documentation address privacy relative to systems development
mitigations.rationale: Formal review of changes helps prevent new privacy weaknesses from being introduced.

mitigations.description: Maintain and publicize the confidentiality safeguards and provide clear notice about how inquiry information is used and protected.
mitigations.evidence_quote: The Ombudsman’s Office also provides notice on its webpage that it has safeguards in place to preserve confidentiality.
mitigations.rationale: Clear notice and confidentiality assurances can reduce chilling effects and support informed participation.

risks.description: The system collects and processes consumer complaints and inquiries that may contain sensitive personal details about a consumer’s financial experiences. Because complaints can be submitted by multiple channels and may include identifiable entities and personal experience, there is a risk of unnecessary exposure or misuse of those details.
risks.evidence_quote: Consumer complaints are submissions that express dissatisfaction with, or communicate suspicion of wrongful conduct by, an identifiable entity related to a consumer’s personal experience with a financial product or service.
risks.rationale: Complaint narratives can reveal personal financial information and dispute details that should be limited to legitimate uses.

risks.description: Physical mail is digitized by vendor staff before being scanned into the system, creating a risk that third-party processors could improperly view, mishandle, or retain complaint documents during intake. This expands access beyond Bureau staff and increases the chance of unauthorized disclosure.
risks.evidence_quote: This refers to digitization of physical mail, where complaints and other documents are sent by consumers to a designated Bureau address for the CRC, processed by vendor staff and immediately scanned into CRS for Bureau use and documentation.
risks.rationale: Vendor handling of incoming mail introduces an additional point where personal information could be exposed.

risks.description: Vendor staff work directly with consumers and process complaints and inquiries on behalf of the Bureau, which creates a risk of overbroad access to consumer information by non-Bureau personnel. If access is not tightly controlled, vendor staff could see more information than needed to provide service.
risks.evidence_quote: Consumer Guides are vendor staff working behalf of the Bureau, who are trained to process complaints and inquiries from consumers. They interact directly with consumers if they choose to speak to a person when calling the CRC contact center.
risks.rationale: Direct handling by contractor staff requires strict least-privilege controls to reduce unnecessary disclosure.

risks.description: The system uses enhanced voice processing such as IVR and automatic computational processing of human languages, which may capture or analyze callers' spoken information in ways consumers do not expect. This creates a risk that voice content could be retained or used beyond the immediate service interaction.
risks.evidence_quote: Tools include enhanced processing of voice communications such as interactive voice response (IVR) - a technology that allows humans to interact with a computer-operated phone system using voice and natural language processing - the automatic computational processing of human languages.
risks.rationale: Voice processing can expose sensitive statements if collection, retention, and access are not constrained.

risks.description: Advanced data analytics are used to assess performance and distill operational improvements, which can create a risk of secondary use of complaint data beyond the original complaint-handling purpose. Even if intended for operations, analytics may still reveal patterns about individual consumers or their complaints.
risks.evidence_quote: Advanced data analytics is a used to assess performance and distill operation improvements.
risks.rationale: Analytics on complaint data can expand use of personal information unless carefully limited and de-identified where possible.

risks.description: The Bureau may send complaints to the company or financial service provider that is the subject of the complaint, to another government agency, or to other offices in the Bureau, which creates a disclosure risk if only the minimum necessary information is not shared. This can expose consumer complaint details to multiple recipients.
risks.evidence_quote: In addressing a complaint or inquiry, Consumer Response may provide additional information to the consumer, send the complaint to the company or financial service provider that is the subject of the complaint, refer the complaint to another government agency, or direct the submission to other offices in the Bureau for further administrative action.
risks.rationale: Sharing complaint records with multiple recipients increases the number of places personal information can travel.

risks.description: Consumer complaints and inquiries are received by phone, physical mail, and email, which creates a risk that information could be intercepted or misdirected during transmission. These channels can expose consumer data if safeguards are not consistently applied across all intake methods.
risks.evidence_quote: Consumer Response receives complaints about financial products and services from consumers via the Bureau’s website, ConsumerFinance.gov/complaint/, by phone, physical mail, and email.
risks.rationale: Multiple intake channels increase the chance of accidental disclosure unless each channel is secured appropriately.

risks.description: The system uses staff identity verification and authentication for access, which indicates that unauthorized access is a relevant risk if credentials are stolen or misused. Because staff email is used for authentication, compromised accounts could expose complaint and inquiry data.
risks.evidence_quote: WFM uses PII for identity verification of staff and the overall operation of the CRC. For example, the email of Bureau staff is used for authentication to obtain access to the CRC system to fulfill their duties.
risks.rationale: Authentication data can be a target for account takeover and should be protected to prevent access to consumer records.

mitigations.description: Limit complaint and inquiry data collection to the minimum information needed to resolve the matter and apply role-based access controls to restrict viewing to staff who need the information.
mitigations.rationale: Minimizing collection and access reduces the chance that sensitive complaint details are exposed or misused.

mitigations.description: Require vendor staff handling physical mail to follow strict handling, confidentiality, and immediate-destruction or secure-transfer procedures, with audit logs for mail intake and scanning.
mitigations.rationale: Tight vendor controls reduce the risk that mailed complaint documents are exposed before they are scanned into the system.

mitigations.description: Impose least-privilege access, confidentiality obligations, and periodic oversight for Consumer Guides so they can access only the consumer information needed to process complaints and inquiries.
mitigations.rationale: Restricting contractor access lowers the likelihood of unnecessary disclosure by vendor staff.

mitigations.description: Provide clear notice to callers when voice communications are processed and limit retention of voice recordings or transcripts to what is necessary for service delivery and quality assurance.
mitigations.rationale: Notice and retention limits help ensure consumers understand and control how their spoken information is handled.
